A GOOD story is worth repeating—but not to the
same man.

THE easiest way to prove that you cannot play the violin is to play it. THE pessimist says, "Things are no better "; the optimist, "Things are no wore." Son E people waste a good .deal of time waiting for the unexpected to happen. THE man who stands on his dignity frequently has a very insecure footing. PHOTOGRAPHY is the art of taking a likeness and changing it into a satisfactory picture. IN one respect the microbe is worthy of imita- tion. It accomplished a gtaat deal before it made any noise in the world. " DOES he joke with his friends?" "No ; persons whom he jokes with are his enemies ever after !" THERE is no reason why a woman shouldn't shine in society if she combines dazzling beauty with brilliant conversation. BROWN: "What is the first thing you have to learn in bicycle-riding—how to mount ? " Jones: No; how to fall so that your injuries will be merely serious, and not necessarily fatal." TIIE way of the transgressor may be hard, but then no one would expect anything else of a road that is travelled so much. DE TANK: "how startling are statistics; we drank seventy million gallons of whisky last year." Mrs. de Tank: "Speak for youyself, please; you know I never touched a drop of It." ELIZA JOHNSON : " areenS Johnson, does yo' know dat yo' fell oaten baid last night ? " Geems Johnson: "Is dat so? Well, I fought I yeered sumpin drop" TEACHER: "Now, Willie, suppose you were to hand a playmate your last apple to take a portion of it, wouldn't you tell him to take the larger piece?" Willie : "No, mom !" Teacher: " You wouldn't! Why !" Willie; "Cos he'd take it, whether or no." "SOMEBODY," she faltered, "may come between us." His breast heaved. "Who ever would do such a thing?' he exclaimed, "would be contemptible small." And with that he moved even yet nearer to her.
"MR. MODDLIN," said that gentleman's wife in a horrified tone, "you are drunk." " Guesh I musht be," assented Modlin cheerfully, "or else I wouldn't (hie) let you see me in this (hic) c'ndshun."

YOUR daughter loves me," urged the youth, "and you refuse to let her have a husband of her own choosing. Yet you say you would deny her nothing." "That," said the old man, grimly, "is exactly what I am doing." "So you called upon that new woman who goes in for athletics," said Plodding Pete. "Yes," replied Meandering Mike, as he stopped rubbing his elbow long enough to tie his handkerchief over his right eye, "I did. An' got a deal the worst of it." Is her husbanicl at home ? " "I dunno. But I hope for his own sake that he ain't." DOBBINS : "I didn't know you had organic heart trouble, Bright's disease, hereditary consumption, and hardening of the liver?" Bobbins: "1 haven't." Dobbins: "But you insinuated as much to that man who just went out." Robbins: "I know. He is a friend of mine and a life insurance agent."

" Oli !" said little Johnny Green, " 'Tis the funniest world e'er seen. For I'm hustled off to bed When no sleep is in my head; And I'm hustled out, you see, When I'm sleepy as can be." A PROVINCIAL assessor recently levied a tax on a citizen's billy-goat, under a regulation which said that all property bounding and abutting on both sides of the street should be taxed so and so. "Faith," said the assessor, " many's the time I've seen that same billy-goat of yours a-boundin' and a-buttin' on both sides o' the street." Sociury Is RED GULCH. - Colonel Shortly French and Miss Rose Jenkins were joined in the holy bonds of matrimony at the residence of the bride's father at ten o'clock last Thursday evening. The ceremony was followed by a recep- tion, at which the elite 1:4 Red Gulch society were present. The gifts were numerous and costly. It gives us great pleasure to announce that Rose will continue to take in washing.
"I TRY very hard to age women," Cried Time; "and, alack ! as you see, The troublesome creatures will near do a thing But make all kinds of faces at me."

CONSOLATION.—A weeping little midshipman, on joining his ship, was thus greeted by the gruff old boatswain: "Come, come, my little man, you must not cry board her majesty's ships of war! Did your mother cry when you left home?" "Yes, sir." "Silly old thing! Did your sister cry when you came away?" "Yes, air." "Stoopid little idiot! Did your father cry when you came away ? " "No sir." "'Ard 'carted old begger !" A CLEVER ROGUE.—Lord Chief Justice Wilmot gave to a party of friends one night a curious account of an innkeeper whom he had tried for having poisoned some of his customers with port wine, by which they narrowly escaped with their lives. It appears that the indictment was quashed through the ilepudence of the prisoner, who absolutely proved that there had never been a drop of real port wine in the hogshead ! Hi 3 uorEs WERE CarSUIED.—A correspondent at Washington tells a story c a well-known naval dignitary who has a beautiful daughter A certain young ensign, with no resources but his slender salary, fell in love with her and asked the old gentleman for her hand. The father at once taxed him with the fact ti,ll. e had only his salary— hardly enough io kf..ep him in white gloves and to burnish his braes but "'Well, Mr. Admiral, what you say is true. But when you married you were only a midshipman, with even a smaller salary than mine. 'Flo \.7 Ui,ou get along?" asked the ensign, who believed he had made the most diplomatic of defences. But not so. The crafty old sea-dog thundered forth: "I lived on my father-in-law for the fitst ten years, but I'll be han4ged if you're going to do it !" /NOTHING TO FRET ABOUT. —An Australian .squatter had the misfortune to shoot one of the aborigines. It was a pure accident, and when the matter was inquired into he was entirly exoner- ated from blame; but being a humane and sen- sitive man, the affair worried him somewhat, and he grew silent and gloomy a state of mind which was the more remarkable, because he had been re- nowned for jollity and light-heartedness. At last his head shepherd, who was much attached to him —for they had come out together from Scotland —received information which he thought would set his master's mind at rest, and hastened to im- part it. "Ye needna greet ony mair aboot the creature you shot, sir," said he, "for I have this vera morning been credibly informed by trust- worthy eye-witnesses that there's hundreds mak of them in the interior of the country." THE BIRD Din NOT FALL—People who were walking along a street not long ago soddenly heard piercing cries from the upper storey of a house. A woman was leaning from a window, and for a moment it was thought that some brute was trying to throw her out. A second look, however, showed that she held in her hand a bird-cage. She had been hanging it out of the window to give her bird the sun, when the bottom dropped out. The startled bird was fluttering about the top of its prison, and the woman was screaming: "Oh, he'll fall—he'll fall ! My poor little birdie !" This was only for a moment. With great presence of mind she turned the cage upside down, so that her pet could not drop out and be dashed upon the cruel pavement. And then the captive went sailing away over the tops of the buildings. For some reason he did not fall. A Social, Phoetmi.—Nodd : "We've got the xisoNt servant-girl we ever had." Todd : "Don't you like her ? " Nodd : "No, sir. The worst of it is, we've got to keep her a week, anyway." Todd: "What's the matter with her ? " Nodd: Ny dear fellow the trouble is not so much in the girl as the people she has lived with. I've always contended that poor servants were the product of bad mistresses. This girl hadn't been with us twelve hours before she showed us plainly that she had been living with the commonest lot of people." Todd : What, did she do that was so bad ?" Nodd: "Do? Why, she slammed doors, talked loud, and as for waiting at table, I never. saw anything like it. As a mere matter of curiosity, I would like to know where that girl has been living." Todd: " I can tea you, old man." Nodd : Where?" Todd " With us for the last year. My wife sent her over u your house."

Since cock-figkting went out of vogue the owners of pedigree fowls have found it diffieult to establish supremacy for a particular breed. The workmen in the proiince of Liege, however, hove discovered a solution of the problem which, if not conclusive, is at any rate ingenious. According to the old adage crowing hens are as little to be encouraged as whistling maids, but the Belgian artisan holds, rightly or wrongly, that the cock which can out- crow its fellows has reached the highest pinnaele of perfection, and crowing contests are now the order of the day. The niqdus operandi is to place the cages containing the roosters in long rows, for it appears that propinquity creates the spirit of emulation without wbich the proceedings would fall flat. A marker appointed by the organisers of the show is told off for each bird, his duty being to note care- fully the number of crows for which he is responsi- ble, in the same fashion as the lens are recorded in a bicycle race. The record so far is held by an English chanticleer which crowed 134 times in the hour, and even then showed no signs of fatigue. The nearest approach to this-130—was reached by - I,ot on Italian bird in the same match. div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

Great efforts are being made in the dockyards to finish the war vessels that should be ready for their steam trials this autumn. The necessity for work- ing overtime has been disputed, and quite recently an order went forth from Whitehall against the practice, but as several yards overtime is being worked on new ships in order to get them ready before the time in which they were to be completed comes to an end. This will mean extra expense, but the money may be saved in other ways. The new warships will be put into commission as soon as they have completed their trials, and some of the ships they supersede may be transferred to the reserve.

The question of ranges for rifle practice is said to be seriously engaging the attention of the War Office, and not before it was time. The Lee-Metford rifle will be issued early in the year, and it will then become imperative to find larger and better ranges.or we shall have constant accidents reported. The rifles are all ready for issue, some 170,000, and the new bullet's penetrative power will then be tested by the Volunteers. In all probability it will go thfough most of the butts at present in use whenever it misses the actual target. If that be the ease a serious state of things will arise.

Before he left London Li Hung Chang received information from his Government, that he would be met at Yokohama by two Chinese warships. He will leave the mail steamer for one of these, and they will sail from Yokohama at once for China, landing the distinguished passenger probably about the 10th of October. An attention like this on the part of the Emperor of China, rather confirms the Viceroy's own anticipation that he may be in full power again before very long.

The Colonial Secrotary is evidently disposed to treat Mr. Maclean's outburst with indifference. This would probably be well enough if Mr. Maclean stoou alone, but it is notorious that the member for Cardiff has only put in very strong language what a number of Conservatives have been thinking and even saying among themselves for some time past with regard to Mr. Chamberlain's colonial policy. The favour which the main lines of this policy have received at the hands of the public and of the press has to a certain extent silenced his detractors on his own side of the House,but they have been rendered none the less bitter by this fact. Their grievance is, of course, in the first place, a personal one. They have never reconciled themselves to seeing Mr. Chamberlain in his present place on the Treasury bench, and if his policy had been a flawless piece of statemanship throughout he would still have had ' his critics both above and below the gangway. In the second place—though this applies to a narrower ' clique—they are furiously angry at what they regard as Mr. Chamberlain's harsh treatment of Mr. Rhodes.

The same people, by the way, have never ceased assailing the Lord Chief Justice for his summing up in the Jameson trial. Again, a large section of the Conservatives strongly resent the appointment of the South Africa Committee, which they regard as a surrender to Sir William Harcourt ; and, whatever course the inquiry by the Committee may take, it will inevitably meet with ridicule and contumely from a number of the supporters of the Government which appointed it. The worst of it is that there are members of the Committee itself who make no secret of their scepticism as to its prcceedings hav- ing any practical result.

From time to time the system of privileged cabs at London railway stations haa raised a growl in Parliament, but without result: and now the cabbies in general are so sore about it they talk of striking. owing to the large number of railway stations, it is a big question—how big may be roughly gathered from the fact that a charge of 21. to Bd. a day for each cab enables the rai.way com- panies to make an average anirial profit of £1,200, after paying checkers and allowing for other ex- penses. The companies say that the system is for the convenience and safety of the public. Jehu denies it, maintaining that the only result is to re- duce his scanty earnings. He is supported by the Small Masters' Association, and both point to the fact that at Waterloo.the only great London station where there have been no privileged cabs for thirty years, vehicles are never lacking and luggage is not lost. The charge of a penny for each cab entering the yard at that terminus is not objected to.

Protests, notwithstanding, the proposed changes in the uniform of army officers have now. I find, receives the formal sanction of Her Majesty. These changes are in the direction of economy. The bearskin flounce for cavalry officers' horses, for ex- ample, except for the Brigade of Guards. is abol- ished. This decoration has been one of the most .expensive items in a cavalry-man's equipment. rile fact that Lord Wolseley has resolutely proceeded with these changes is interpreted in military circles to mean that he will carry out his general purpose to the full.

Great reticence, for some T eason or other, is ob- served respecting the stay of the Empress of Russia at Balmoral. It was the Empress's intention to remain with the Queen after the Czar's departure, but some pressure has been put upon the Czar to take the Czarina to France with him, and it almost looks as if it would be successful. If this were the case the Imperial pair would pass through London, and it would be hardly possible to avoid the public demonstration which it has been desired to obvi- ate, though it could not be anything more than a display of popular feeling in the streets and at the railway stations. In anticipation of such events a large number of Russian police have been for some time in London. They find everything very quiet indeed at present, no Nihilists having recently left the continent for this country.

Since Peter the Hermit there hasfnot been a more picturesque clergyman than the Rev. T.C. curate of Spitalfields,whose compulsory resignation has thrown many of the East End poor into con- sternation. A faint idea of what he is may be gathered from the names by which the people know him—" The Dossers' Parson," " The Smoking Parson," and so on. His exceedingly unconven- tional ways have more than once drawn protests frc m the orthodox,but he has remained indifferent. Now, however, he is obliged to take heed, for the new vicar objects. His ordinary offences lie in socialistic views and in preaching in Baptist and Methodist meeting houses, but as the new vicar. and presumably the patron, are ritualistic, it is pro- bable that" Parson Collings," as he calls himself, committed the deadly sin during the last school board elections when he went about deciouncing sacerdotalism with more strength of language than the Puritans applied to the Romish Church. Even the Establishment he fiercely attacked for standing in the way of educating the poor. His zeal for the poor is a passion. What he calls " Bible, bacca, and baked tater evenings" are amongst his means of reaching them. He has informed some of his humbla friends that he will soon be a scavenger for the Whitechanel Board of Works. It is said that a Liberal peer offered him a chaplaincy SOMQ time ago, but he refused because he preferred labour among the lowly.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 29. 1896
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 29. 1896

" Afier I got well," continued Mrs. Narr, hurriedly, avertiug her eyes, "I took a baby to nurse, hoping that the money I should get for it would help us and encourage Jack. Its father—a great and rich lord—he's been minister abroad since—paid liberal. He thought the world of the little heiress, whose mother lay ill for months of a fever. But Jack was past being encouraged. He went on from had to worse. And at last—it was the day my lord's baby died "—and the woman's voice trembled—" the tenant of whom we hired our little farm sent us notice of ejectment. That, and the trouble of the baby's death, fired Jack to desparation. He must have been drinking when he did it, but he forged the tenant's name for three hundred pounds. He got the money—more than we had ever seen at one time—and after that, of course, nothing remained but flight. The baby was hastily buried, and Jack and I fled with our little one.' _ _ _ _
Her voice trembled, and again she looked plead- ingly at Dora, whose face shone out of the cool grey dusk like a face chiselled from marble. "And then?" said Dora, as the woman continued silent.

"And then," said Mrs. Narr, in a broken voice, "there followed a season of wandering. Jack and I, with the baby, went from one country town to another, fancying that the officers of the law were on our track. A step behind us, a hand on our shoulder, or a voice suddenly accosting us, was enough to scare us out of our senses. In the hop season we picked hops in Kent. Sometimes we worked on farms, and sometimes we idled whole weeks away, living on the money Jack had gained by forgery. Our life of constant tear told on us. At last Jack used to say that he'd rather die than be always dodging and always hightened at his own shadow. He got thin and pale and nervous, and finally we saw that we must leave the country. We had not dared to go at first, fearing that the officers would watch for us at every port. It was when we had made up our mind to go—when we were on our way to London to embark—that we came to the little hamlet down yonder."
At this point in her narrative she arose and walked back and forth; her agitation _increasing.

"The baby was ien a year:. old," she continUed, "and as fair and delicate as a little lily. I used to take pride in keeping her sweet and clean, she was so dainty. We had a hundred and thirty pounds left of the three hundred got by the forgery. We put up at the inn down at the hamlet over night, and the next morning we set out to tramp it to London. We were well on our way, quite near the Grange, when a carriage came slowly along. Squire Chessom was in it, with his pretty lady wife. We stopped, out of curiosity to look at the great people, and as we did so the baby, whom I had set on her little feet, put up her pretty arms to the lady and crowed in baby fashion. "Then the lady says : What a lovely little creature 1' and tells her husband to stop the carriage. And she must have the baby up to speak to her, and she said she had a son away at school, and she wished she had a little daughter, like this child. Then Jack speaks, quick-like, and says she might have this one, for we were going to Canada, and she was in our way. Then the lady and her husband talked together, and the child clung to the lady as if she had found her home. And the long and short of it was that the squire gave Jack and me a hundred pounds to stock a farm in Canada, and he took the child, saying he should bring it up as his own. And that every day the squire and his wife went away travelling, taking the baby, and intending to be gone a long time, so that no one should suspect when they came back that the child was not their own. And three days afterward Jack and I sailed for Canada." Dora's gaze wavered now, and she turned away her head. She was beginning, in spite of herself, to believe the woman's story. Mrs. Narr, with a quick, keen glance at the slight, bowed figure, resumed: "We got a farm in Canada, and other children were born to us. But Jack's bad habits stayed by him, and the farm was mortgaged, and finally sold, and we lived from hand to mouth. Once I wrote to Squire Chessom for fifty pounds, and he sent it; but he told me not to write again, as he should answer no more letters. The ohildren died off one by one, and last year Jack died, leaving me poor and in debt. Then my heart turned to my first- born, the only being I had left to cling to. I worked as a house-servant in Montreal until I had earned enough to bring me back to England; and here I am, Dora. I arrived here this morning, and made cautious inquiries about you. You will not refuse to recognise me now ? " She came nearer to the girl. There was a short, sharp conflict in Dora's soul. The precision, exactness and earnestness of the woman impressed her with a sense of her truthful-

ness. She stood up, trembling with a terrible agitation. "You will kiss me, Dora ?" pleaded the woman. " YOZI will call me mother 2" She came a step nearer. Again Dora put up her hands to ward off her approach. The girl had a warm, true and impulsive heart. She was without vain pride and self-love. It was not the woman's poverty or rank in life that repelled her, but she could not kiss her, she could not call her by the name she had given to the dead Mrs. Chessom. Her whole nature rose up against this claimant on her filial love. Her instinct recoiled from her. "I cannot 1" she panted. "You must not come nearer to me ! I can never call you mother I" ," Dora !" "That name was given to me by one who is now dead, but who during all my life never let me sus- pect that I was not born of her. The name Is sacred, and I cannot give it to you." "Oh, my child !" Dora grew calmer. "If your story is true," she said, "you cannot object to my telling it to—to my father," and she spoke the name firmly, half defiantly. "If he says It is true, we will then talk the matter over. If he says it is not true—" She paused, and her heart sank within her. Her conversation with the squire that morning, and his mysterious allusions to his son, Edmund, as her possible lover, came back to her with chilling force. "He will say that it is true," said Mrs. Narr, "even if he blames me for telling you." "You had better remain here for the present, until you hear from me," said Dora, striving to speak leas coldly than heretofore. "I will talk the matter over with papa this evening. To- morrow you shall hear from us. If—if what you say is true, you shall be cared for and helped. But It will be well for you, until you hear what papa says, to say nothing to any one else concerning this matter. Mrs. Narr made profuse assurances that she had said nothing concerning her relationship to Miss Chessom since her arrival, and that she should continue to be guarded on the subject. "I don't want to make any trouble," she said, volubly. "I have had a hard life, and all I want now is an easy one. I don't want to take you from the Grange, if that can be avoided. I have got no child but you to support me, and I want you to do It. If the squire will pension me off, I'll agree to be as discreet as I have always been." These words seemed to the hearer more mercenary than motherly. They chilled her. "I do not recognise your claims upon the child you sold for money," was her response. " What— what papa will think, I don't know. But what- ever he does in the matter will be just and right. And one thing more," she added, sternly. "You can never take me from the Grange—never He who has sheltered and loved and cared for me all my life has the strongest claims upon me, and I will never desert him for a .stranger, let that stranger be a thousand times my mother. The accident of birth is nothing compared to the num- berless kindnesses he has showered upon me 1" A look of anger flamed up into Mrs. Narr's eyes. "There were no papers executed, giving you away," she exclaimed. "You are but seventeen, and I, as your mother, am your rightful guardian. It will be better for you not to get on your high. heeled boots with me. A pretty greeting this is for your mother. I came to you with a bleeding heart, but you are like an iceberg. You sneer at my love. You may not be able to sneer at my authority." "All this can he discussed after I have seen papa," said Dora, calmly. "As I said, you will, without doubt, hear from him to-morrow." She bowed quietly, opened the door, and passed out. The next moment she was hurrying down the stairs into the outer air. She felt strangely weak and tired. The glare of the sunlight annoyed her, and she turned into the now empty tea-garden, and sat down in its shaded arbour to recover her strength and her thoughts. "That woman my mother !'' she thought. "And her husband, the runaway forger and drunkard, my father! Oh, Heaven! And I have been so proud of my honourable lineage! And papa—dear papa-- is not my father! How can I bear it 1' The thought brought the anguished tears to her eyes. She looked around her piteously, as an entrapped bird looks for some loop-hole of escape. At last. hearing one of the stable lads approach-

OR, A WAR OF THE HOUSEHOLD,
Dy the Author of "The Double Lifo," "The BAilift's Scheme," &c., &c.
CHAPTER 111. DIRS. NARR.

The narrow country road leading past Chessom Grange and the Hare and Hounds inn, and travers- ing the pretty little hamlet half a mile beyond, was one of the pleasantest roads to be found in all the fair Weald of Sussex. It was bordered on either side by hawthorn hedges, now in a very profligacy of bloom, looking as if heaped with wanton snow- drifts. In the shadow of the hedges, close to the beaten footpath, were flaunting scarlet poppies, primroses, and dog-roses, and the fragrant breaths of the latter mingled with the sweet scent of the hawthorn blooms, perfuming the warm and sunny air.

For the first time in her young life Dora Chessom heeded neither the flowers, the fragrance, nor the sunshine. The dazed feeling yet lingered in her brain, and the shadow of a great trouble brooded yet more heavily about her soul. She put the crushed note in her pocket and walked on briskly, gradually regaining her usual calmness and presence of mind. She was quite herself when she came in sight of the inn, and slackened her pace, assuming a quiet exterior, This inn was a quaint old building, with diamond paned casement window, and a long, low porch in front. A row of benches lined this porch, and at the side of of the inn in a shaded tea-garden, were more benches and little wooden tables, and a rustic arbour, arranged for the entertainment of the people Of the neighbouring hamlet and the whole country side, for the Hare and Hounds was a favourite resort with the thriving yeomanry of the region. Dora turned into the tea-garden, where a stout maid was at work polishing the tables-, and approach- ing the woman, inquired for Mrs. Narr—that, as the reader remembers, being the name appended to the singular note she had so recently received. "Mrs. Narr !" repeated the serving-woman, rather stupidly. "Oh, that be the stranger woman in the two pair back. Yes, Miss. She be in the parlour waiting for company. I'll show you the way." With an air of great respect, for the squire's pretty daughter was well known throughout the neighbourhood, the woman conducted Dora along the porch, into the cool hall, and upstairs, where she halted, pointing at the parlour door. "She be in there, Miss, she whispered. "Go right in. She'll be glad enow to see your sweet face, for she needs help, I'm thinking." With this the maid hurried down the stairs, her goloshes clattering at every step. Dora advanced to the parlour door and knocked, her heart fluttering like a prisoned bird. A voice answered from within the room, bidding her enter. For a moment the girl hesitated, vainly wishing that retreat were possible. If only she had not obeyed that strange summons! If only she had waited and shown the letter to her father. Repressing resolutely her misgivings, Dora opened the door and entered the parlour. The blinds were lowered, shutting out the sun- light. Dora paused near the door to accustom her eyes to the gloom. The casement windows were open, swinging inward like doors. The floor uncarpeted, was of oak, black as ebony and polished like glass. An antique set of furniture, finely polished also, adorned the sides of the room. The grate was concealed by an elaborate curtain of gay tissue papers, festooned in ringlets, and trailing upon the fender. A black- framed mirror hung over the high mantel-piece, and a few similarly framed silhouettes adorned the walls. All these features Dora observed before her quick glances detected, upon a high, straight-backed re fa, in the cool half-dusk of a farther corner, a woman's figure. She had scarcely discovered this presence, before the woman arose and came forward to meet her. "You are Mrs. Narr ?" asked Dora, with quiet girlish dignity, and with a steady self-possession that surprised herself. "I am," was the reply, in an eager voice, "You got my note? You are Dora ?" "lam Miss Chessom," replied Dora, with an un- conscious hauteur. The woman uttered a quick exclamation, crossed the floor and drew up the blind, letting in a flood of light. She then approached her visitor, halted, and the two looked at each other fixedly. Mrs. Narr was a tall, well-formed country-looking woman, decently attired, yet evidently intimately acquainted with poverty. Her countenance was commonplace—one of those ordinary, stolid faces which betray so little of the real character of their possessor. Her complexion was singularly sallow, and her eyes, keen restless, and glittering with eagerness, seemed keen, to devour the object upon which they were now fixed. It seemed as if Dora's appearance surprised her. This slender, graceful figure in its stylish short walking suit of white linen striped with black, sur- mounted by the radiantly beautiful face, was evi- dently not what she expected to see. "You are Dora ? " she repeated, seeming in- credulous. The young girl bowed coldly Dad gravely. The woman came a step nearer, hesitated, and then held out her arms, while a tremulous smile flickered about her lips. "You read my note?" she said, hurriedly. "You know that you are my child? Oh, Dora! Dora 1" But Dora shrank back from the proffered embrace' her face deadly pale, and her eyes glow- ing with strange intensity. " Do not touch me 1" she said, putting up her hands. "I read your note, but of course, there is some mistake. I am the daughter of Squire Chessom, of the Grange, and of his wife, who died three years ago. Papa had just gone to Horsham when your note came, or I should have shown it to him at once, despite your request. You see how impossible it is that your story can be true." The woman's arms dropped to her side. "Then you never suspected that you were not Squire Chessom's daughter ?" she exclaimed. "Of course not. Why should I suspect anything so strange and preposterous?" "Then they have indeed been tender and kind to you, as they promised," said Mrs. Narr. "Heaven bless them !"

Dora's face grew stern in its hrigbt young beauty. "You must not talk in that way to me," she said. "I cannot allow you to speak to me as though you were my mother. lam not certain that I have done right in coming here, but I desired to prevent any scandal in the neighbourhood." "I do not wonder that you refuse to believe my assertions," said the woman, humbly and depre- catingly. "But, at least, listen to me. Hear what I have to say, and then judge for yourself. I can prove the truth of my story.' She drew forward a chair for the young lady, motioning her by a gesture to occupy it. Dora hesitated. She was heartily sorry that she bad obeyed the strange summons of this woman, end yet she could no longor look upon her as an tatter impostor. There was an air of sincerity about Mrs. Narr that impressed the girl singularly and uncomfortably. With one steady, searching look .into the light ,ensyeou. secured h blue eyes of her hostess Dora sat down, saying: s•I woman l hear e6tt)oent. The he door and lowered the blind, and then sat down near Dora, in the grey half dusk. Little bars of sunlight stole in through the interstices of the blinds, along with the hum of bees, the song of birds, the cool breeze an he cheery song of the maid in the tea-garden below. • For a few minutes there was silence between the two women. Then Mrs. Narr spoke, in a subdued tone: "Let me begin at the commencement, Dora. Somehow I don't feel free to talk to you, who have been educated like a lady. I am only a country-woman--a simple, ignorant country-woman —and you are far above me, if you are my own child. When I was a girl, of your age, I was lady's maid to the wife of a famous doctor in Lon- don. I lived with her till I was twenty, and then I married Jack Narr, who kept a public house down in Surrey. We did pretty well at that for a while, but Jack took to drinking up the stock, and I was afraid he would become a eot, so I persuaded him to hire a small farm of a man who had taken

two, and who was willing to sub-let this one reasonable. Jack did pretty well on the farm for a while, but by-and-by he went back to his old companions aua took to drinking, and the farm went behindhand, so that the tenant of whom we hired it threatened to turn us out. It was at about that time, when everything was going wrong, that my baby was born." She paused, with a pleading look at Dora, whose large 'bright eyes never swerved in their fixed acrutini of her fe,ce.

ing, and -not wishing to be seen there loijer, she wiped her eyes, arose and went out of the garden into the public road. She had gone but a few paces, her step languid, her head drooping, when she heard the sound of a horse's hoofs behind her, and then a fresh and Pleasant voice calling her name.
CHAPTER IV. A THREATENING LOOK-OUT.

Lord Champney took possession of the chamber assigned him at the Saltair Manor, remaining within it an hour or more, by which time his luggage had arrived from Cromer. At the end of the period named he came forth, ascertained that a messenger had been dispatched to Norwich with his telegram to his kinsman, Mr. Felix Warner, and then ordered his horse and rode away at a furious pace, taking the coast road to Yarmouth. He was absent several hours, returning late in the afternoon. The Lady Barbara's guepts, attired for dinner, were gathered on the lawn, sitting on the rustic seats under the trees, or strolling idly along the cool and shaded paths. Lord Champney passed them swiftly, just noticing that the Lady Barbara was not among them, and dismounted at the porch, hastening to his own chamber. He was nearly exhausted with his long and furious ride, and with the passions which had raged tumultuously in his breast from the moment of meeting his wife after their long separation. The sight of her in her glorious beauty had swept away all the coldness and the bitterness of years. and he loved her with a passion which alarmed himself. He rang his bell and flung himself on a couch, a feeling of languor creeping over his tired frame. A servant speedily appeared, and Lord Champ- ney demanded if any response had as -yet been received to the telegram he had sent to town. "No, my lord," replied the servitor, respect- fully; "the messenger has not got back. He was to wait fot an answer, my lord, and it's nigh twenty miles to Norritch." "Very well," said Lord Champney. "Let me know when the messenger comes. You may go." The servant withdrew, and the baron knitted his brows, as he was wont to do when annoyed. "As likely as not, Felix is out of town again," he muttered. "He met me in London two days since as I telegraphed him from Paris, but told me he had business down in Sussex and must go back. What can his business be? He has been staying at or near Horsham for the past three months— ever since he left me in Germany. Can he have fallen in love at last, I wonder ?" He smiled at the bare suggestion. After a little he arose, attired himself with the scrupulous care of a man who respects himself and the opinions of others, and then sauntered to the window which was open, the blinds being closed. He looked out through the moveable shutters upon the group beneath. The guests had gathered themselves upon circular seats under a spreading acacia, and were in the midst of a merry discus- sion. Lord Champney regarded them keenly. While he looked, the Lady Barbara came out and joined them. They welcomed her eagerly, making room for her in their midst. The husband's eyes filled with tears at sight of her. How royally she bore herself How fair and stately she was in her floating robe of black grena- dine, and with her pale gold hair gathered high at the back of her head, after the prevailing style, and ornamented with a jet comb. "Can that be Barbara—my wife ?" thought his lordship, womderingly. "I left her a pretty girl- -1 find her a magnificent woman. It seems as if she had put on mourning because of my return. Ah, she hates me now as she once loved me! I wonder what Felix would say to her now. I owe it to him that my eyes were opened to her perfidy —or to what we believed to be her perfidy. Poor Felix 1 He never liked Barbara, and he has always advised me to never see her again. I did not tell him I was coming hers. I wonder what he will say when he discovers lam at Sal tair. No doubt he will think me weak and foolish. Felix was always jealous of my dignity. He never believed that Barbara loved me. He—" _ _ _

He paused aln:Uptii as Willard Ames joined the group on the lawn, and threw himself upon the close-shaven grass at the Lady Barbara's feet. His lordship did not notice that the Lady Bar- bara's niece sat beside her—indeed, he did not know her niece from the other ladies. He only noticed that Mr. Ames was smiling up into her ladyship's face, and the demon of jealousy—the demon that had desolated his life and that of the Lady Barbara—awoke from his slumbers and sprang up into fierce, new life within him, as the deadly hydra arouses from its slumbers into a veno- mous activity." " Ah ! " he said, breathing hard, his handsome face darkening. "I came home in good time. My lady is too fair and faithless to be trusted entirely with the care of my name! I must look after it and her myself. Why, I heard that she lived at Saltair in a perfect seclusion? I heard this a hundred times —the double-playing coquette! I wonder how often Ames has visited her! This is her seclusion— all these guests to afford a pretext for the visit of Willard Ames! Her niece lives with her as a cover, and as a shield against the suspicions of the world They are clever—but they shall find that I also am clever 1" He struggled with his emotions, schooling his features to a bitter and cynical expression. Then, taking up his hat, he went below, making his way out to the group on the lawn. The Lady Barbara arose at his approach, welcom- ing him with a quiet though cold salutation. She was a proud woman, proud to her heart's core. Not for worlds would she have had her guests know of the state of affairs between her hus- band and herself. At the luncheon table she had quietly announced Lord Champney's resignation of his post abroad, and his return to England, and his presence at Saltair; and no one, except Willard Ames, not even her niece, suspected that this return was unwelcome to her. The announcement had created quite a flutter among the guests, Lord Ciarinpney's reputation as a diplomatist ranking high. They looked up now, as he came near, with ill-concealed curiosity and deference. The Lady Barbara hastened to effect the neces- sary introductions. "Lady Clara Howe, Lady Augusta Howe, Lord Champney," she said, with a quiet grace. The returned minister bowed deeply to the fair twin sisters, who were daughters of Lord Howe, formerly his intimate friend. "And this," said the Lady Barbara, as a tall, fair, sweet-faced girl arose, blushing and smiling, this young lady, Lord Champney, is my niece, Ada Gower. She rn,ust have grown entirely out of your remembrance.' Lord Chempney gave his hand to Miss Gower, and expressed his delight at meeting her again, she having been a little child when he had last seen her. The gentlemen, Mr. Tillinghast, and Captain Burton of the Guards, both profusely wiskered young men of the most fashionable stripe, and both of them devoted admirers of the Howe sisters, on whose account they had been invited to Saltair, were then introduced to Lord Champney, who greeted them with polite cordiality. " I am last but not least," said Willard Ames, coming forward with a smile. "Let me hope that no introduction is necessary to recall me to Lord Charnpney's mind. Welcome home, my lord." He held out his hand with boyish frankness. For a single instantthe baron hesitated, haughtily disinclined to accept it. But he was as proud as the Lady Barbara, and choking down his anger and resentfulness, he held out his hand in a lifeless fashion, permitting Ames to grasp it, which he did heartily. "I do remember you, Mr. Ames," he said, stiffly, and with a significance meant to strike and appal two of his hearers. "I have a good memory for my friends and my enemies alike! I never forget a kindness—l never forget an injury." His eyes blazed with a gloomy fire as he looked intently at the man he hated. Willard Ames looked back at him, his honest blue eyes full of a frank and friendly spirit, the integrity of his manly soul shining from his delicate and effeminate features. A moment they stood thus; then Willard dropped the hand he held, sighing. Willard Ames was a distant cousin of the Lady Barbara, and had been her father's ward. From their childhood the two, who were of like age, had been like brother and sister. They had played to- gether and studied together until Willard had been sent to Eton, and the separation that then occurred had not had power to weaken their mutual affection. Their love had never changed its character, and Willard had kept up his fraternal intercourse with the Lady Barbara after her marriage, never dream- ing that the jealous husband suspected him of being the lover of one whom he regarded as his sister. Then came the baron's outbreak of moody jealousy without a cause, and the Lady Bar- bara told her kinsman that he must visit her no more. Worked upon by an artful and de- signing relative, Felix Warner—he who was now lingering in Sussex as the lover of innocent Dora Chessotn, Lord Champney then believed that his wife and Willard Ames met each

other in secret. At this crisis, the Lady Barbaraa illness and the birth of their child for a time effec- ted a diversion in the mind of the baron; but his jealousy returned with tenfold force when he found among his wife's most cherished possessions a packet of love-letters to which was appended the name of Willard Ames.

Then, maddened into a desperate fury, Lord Champney, as has been said, had proposed an " amicable " separation to his wife. She acceded, and they had since walked in separate life-paths. After Lord Champney'b departure, the Lady Bar- bara had dwelt at Saltair in the utmost circum- spection, so that not even her worst enemy, Felix Warner, could find aught to say in her dispraise. She had never permitted Willard Ames to visit her ; but she and her niece had often met him, and Willard had learned to love Ada, who was as yet ignorant of his passion. It was to bring these two loved ones together, and to give Willard a fair chance for his wooing, that the Lady Barbara had invited her present company. It was a terrible mistake.

So the Lady Barbara felt it, under all her proud seeming, when her husband turned from Ames aud, with a forced smile on his lips and a black shadow brooding in his eyes, addressed himself in courteous coldness to Miss Gower.

"This is a pleasant coming home, Miss Ada," he observe.:, his every word reach;ng his wife's ears as he inteLded they should. " Delightful ! Ah, it is in the greeting a man receives after a long absence that tells him how his family regard him. I never knew myself so rich in affection. I shall never go abroad again to stay. Henceforth my home shall be in England with my family." Ada Gower thought the words natural and kindly. The Lady Barbara knew that they were meant to stab her heart like so many arrows.

She grew a little paler, and murmuring some- thing about the closeness of the air, walked toward the cliff, upon the verge of which was a stone balustrade. She reached the balustrade and leaned heavily upon it, looking seaward with eyes that saw nothing. _ _ _

Her husliand and Willard Ames both noticed her departure, and the strange Quiver that shook her slender figure as she stood on the cliff, her light garments fluttering in the breeze. The heart of the former yearned over her with a great and rassionate love. He would have given worlds, had he possessed them, to gather her to his heart, and know her to be true and faithful to him, and to know that she also loved him. He would have followed her, but his pride withheld him. Willard Ames quietly took measures that her ladyship's withdrawal from the group should not be noticed. _ _

"'rho Lady Augusta's bouquet is withered," he observed, picking up a flower that had dropped from it. • "That is a bad omen, Captain Burton, if we remember the pretty speech you made when you plucked it." "Nonsense, Ames," cried the captain, redden- ing, yet striving to speak gaily. "I'd never base my hopes upon the lives of such frail flowers as those. 'I know a bank' of flowers that might fitly offer types of affection. Come with me into the flower-garden," he added, with a significant glance at Miss Gower, "and I will show you for your own benefit." "If you are going that way, just bring them to me," said Ames, with an affectation of laziness, and an admirable imitation of the captain's drawl. "The day is too sultry for much exertion." _ _ _
The captain laughed, offered his arm to the Lady Augusta, and the two strolled away toward the flower-garden. The Lady Clara and Mr. Tillinghast followed them. _ _ _
Lord Champney, Ames, and Ada Gower were thus left on the lawn, the first and the last engaged in conversation.

Ames approached the Lady Barbara. He was at her side before she marked his approach. She started as he leaned beside her on the balustrade, crossing his arms before him, and stole a glance over her shoulder in sudden appre- hensiveness. _ _ _

Yes, as she had instantly feared, Lord Champney was looking at them with a brow like night, while he made smiling remarks to Ada. "Barbara," said Willard, reading her husband's surveillance in her suddenly dilating eyes, "has that man begun where he left off years ago when you two parted? Has he resumed his wicked, causeless jealousy ?" "Oh, hush, hush, Willard l" uttered the Lady Barbara with a shiver. "Remember he is my husband." "That is no reason why he should make you miserable !" exclaimed Willard, in a suppressed voice. "That he is your husband is reason that he should respect and exalt you. I must speak plainly. Am I not your brother in all but the tie of blood? Did not your father on his deathbed enjoin me to shield you and care for you as if you were my own sister?" _ _ .

- "Yes, Willard, and I regard you as my brother. You have brightened my life—my lonely, desolate life." "Am I to go away?" asked Willard, "Will it be better if I go over to Cromer to-night ?" "No. If you were to go now, Lord Champney would feel that his suspicions were confirmed. Your going would look like flight." "True,' assented Willard, thoughtfully. "Besides," said the Lady Barbara, with a strange out-look at the dancing white cres ts of the restless waves, as they beat against the broken rocks below the cliff, "if you were to leave before the rest of the party, there might be wonder and gossiping. The others will only be here three or four days longer. You will stay ?" "I will stay, Barbara." "After the others go, you know, you can go to Cromer. He cannot suspect any evil if you stay there, for Cromer is a watering-place, and just now it is unusually full. I feel as if I would like to have you near me—although, perhaps, it would be better to send you away. I feel strangely troubled, Willard. It is about Colonel Effingham. He is at Cromer again." Willard Ames started. "Again ?" he repeated. "He has annoyed you enough, Barbara. The scoundrel 1" The Lady Barbara's cheek flushed. "Lord Champney was jealous of him also, in the old days," she said. "He knew that Colonel Effingham had offered me his hand, and that I had refused him. The colonel's marriage, however, had quieted his suspicions in that direction. But the colonel's wife is dead now, and Heaven only knows the peril that lies before me. Some enemy of mine —Felix Warner, I believe, for I am sure Warner is my secret enemy—told Colonel Etliugha.m last year that Sidney and I had parted, and that the cause of our separation was that my hus- band made the discovery that I loved the col- onel, whom I had not seen since I rejected him. Preposterous as the infamous story was Colonel Effingham had the incredible vanity to believe it. He came up to Cromer. He called upon me. He has persecuted me with letters, flowers, and gifts, all of which I have sent back to him—all the letters, save the first one, unopened. The fact that I have lived here all those years alone, while my husband has lived abroad, seems to outweigh all my haughtiness, all my coldness, all my indignation. I have ceased to recognize him when %Vs) meet—but here he is back at Cromer. 1 could almost believe that some secret enemy of mine—Felix Warner, perhaps has bribed the colonel to infuriate my husband,--and to—to try to compromise me in my husband's sight." "That suggestion throws a flood of light on the matter," said Ames. "We can talk of that here- after. But now Barbara, I think you ought to go away 1" "I can't go anywhere that Colonel Effingham cannot follow," ssid the Lady Barbara, bitterly. "And you dare not tell this trouble—to Lord Champney? Poor Barbara 1 I do not see that I can help you." And Willard Ames sighed heavily. "Let me think the matter over. I will try to hit upon some plan for your protection which shall not compromise you, arouse a scandal, or awaken your husband's suspicion. Meet me at this spot after the others have retired to-night, Barbara, and we will talk this matter over fully. Meanwhile, trust in me." "I shall not dare meet you in secret, Willard," said the Lady Barbara. "It is not like me to do anything secret." "Can you meet me openly, Barbara ?" "No. You know I can't. I will come, Willard, for I cannot manage this affair myself, and I am afraid that something may come to Sidney's ears. Well as you know him, you cannot imagine how terrible Lord Champney is when maddened by his evil passion." And the wife shuddered. " I will be here at eleven. By that time the house will be quiet." At this juncture a step was heard on the lawn behind them. Starting, they turned, and beheld Lord Champney, his face drawn and convulsed with ' bitter rage. "Ah !" he exclaimed, with sarcastic emphasis, I "Near nave (ikturbed you. I beg your p trdon. " ' Lady Barbara look quickly round her, fearing

lest his lordship's words -should be overheard. The guests were still in the flower garden. Ada, Gower had gone into the house. "You do not disturb us, Sidney," said his wife' with a forced and sickly smile. "We shall be glad of your company." "Oh, no doubt !" sneered the baron. glad! You look so! But I have nothing to say W you. I desire a private interview with Mr. Ames' If he is a gentleman he will not refuse it." There was a deep menace in his lordship's tones' and a deep menace in his eyes. The Lady Barbara trembled, but she dared pet speak. I.lr words could not pour oil en the troubled waters. "I am willing to grant the interview you seek, my lord," said Ames, proudly. "There goes the dinner-bell. We will dine first—to keep up apPeBr- ances before the Lady Barbara's guests—and thel I shall be happy to hear what you have to FAY ID me." Lord Champney ! owed a cold assent, and the three moved towards the house, the guests comla from the garden to join them. (To be continued).

The fine woven fancy canvas is a woaderfully effective fabric, especially in the new meLberry and dark red shades. The want of summer is already marked by the subtle change to be nottd in modes of the moment. Muslims and chiffoirs are giving place to more substantial materials, and neat tailor coats are again wearable over thin blouses. The newest coats are of the severest cut; and I saw one the other day at a leaditg tailor's which was straight-fronted, quite plain., minus even a visible button, and had small t)lain coat sleeves without a vestige of fulness at the 4houlders— exactly like those of a man's coat.

"WOMEN'S CHAT." The accepti.nce n't Bushey House, Bushey Park,br the Duke and Duch eisis of York, is to be attributed to the t strong desire of tier Royal Highness to be within readt of Richmond. It is &picturesque, old4ashioned house., with pretty xrounds,which are finely timbered. BuArey was for alcmg time the residence of the Duke and Duchess cr. Clarence (William IV. and Queen Adelaide), and frontl.B37 it was the dower house at the 'Queen
Dowager until her death in 1849, when the place was 2ranted to tha late Due de Nemours._ The Duchesse do . _
iVemoors, who died in 1857, was a first cousin of the

iQueen and of Prince Albert. The Duchess of Fife is keeping up her reputation this yeaT,as an expert fisherwoman, at Mar Lodge. She has lately caught some fine salmon weighing trom five to +nine pounds. It is a favourite amusement with many l'women of high rank. The Princess of Wales ig most en- thusiastic and droit,as is also the Countess of Westmor- land. The latter lady favours both the Tweed. and

Corniderable disappointment is felt among the people of Sterbiton, a favourite river-side resort of Londoners at tire news that the marriage of the Duke ot Orleans and the Australian Archduchees Dorothea, is after all to

take place at the Imperial Palace at Vienna. It was all but:: arranged that the ceremony should be performed in the beautiful little church on the river front at Surbiton vihich has always been so much patronised by exiled trench Royalties of different families. It is said that the Archduchess will bring her future husband a •dowry of seven million francs, and it is also stated that the emperor of Austria's principa: wedding gift to the bride and bridegroom, will be an estate situated in tbe most picturesque part of Hungary. It appears that in 1898, M. Jean de Resyke has finally resolved to abandon the stage, an item of news that will not be a pleasing one to his many admirers. His marri- age is to take place in Poland, early in October, before the eminent singer departs upon his American tour. M. Paderewski's health is once again causing consider- able anxiety. The fatigue of constant travel, no leas than the demands he 'mikes upon himself in his recitals, are doubtless the cause of what is described as a collapse, and the,engagements which have been made for hini,for the earlierpart of next year have had to be cancelled,as the state of his nervono system renders a long rest abso- lutelyinecessary for his restoration to health. As .a merely fashionable institution, th. Royal Academy has iallen -off appreciably since the death of _ . _ . . . . - . .
LoWLeighton,and *le Aca.ciemician-s, in search of a sew president, are divided into two parties. of which one is bent.upon maintaining the fashionable prestige and the
oeher the artistic reptitation of the AcaitemyT The 'date
Sic.Uohn Millais wci elected unanimously at the death of Lord ,Leighton,as tin only man who coufd net be passed

mer;but at the present moment there is no AcadeMician markedly popular, either with the profession,the,pablic, .or with society. The ideal president of course brim who combines the three qualificeions. 'Motor-cars seem likely to have a more considerable in- ifluenee on society than was at first anticipated. livery up-to-datc individual is it appears, building himself a ,motor-house, in which he purposes to travel afiloverthe
country, and tic considers ihai there is no reascra why all houses should not similarly constnected. Vet with all

due deference to the great man's opinion, one cannot help thinkingrt hat a motor-street woold be a comic sight, especially if e7erybody started for the seaside -at the same time. Apropos ofenotor-cars,it is to be sincerely triaged that their adventswill not mean tyred wheels, anda noiseless approach like that of the bicyclist who rings his bell at' three yards distance when travelling at the 'rate of twelve miles an flour. We have, most of us., had many narrow escapes, and unpleasant shooks from the terror on wheels, ‘and if we are to twee noiselessnaotor-cars about the streets, a few more hespitala would appear necessarritams to consider, at ms•early date. With regard to remunerative *employment for poor gentlewomen, there is little doubt that a good liviog could betrtade by those residing in favourite -seaside towns, if !they were to lay themselves ,out -to inspect apartments and cottages for intending visitors. 'Many householders purposing to bringalamily to 'the •seaside, and unabla perhaps to spend a day or two in visiEng the place beforehand, would gladly spend a guinea or half a guinea to obtain an independsnt opinion as to whettierrthe house they are negotiating 'by advertise- ment isViean, free of smells, and otherwise • desirable. As things are now, one is wholNy in the hands Of the local agent, with the result that seaside trips too often mean illness, and if nething serious, an intimate acquaintance with dirt, that spoils the 'holiday. 'Ad ver- tisetnente in the leading papers of all large' towns, to the effect tie-A apartments or houses could be found, or in- spected., would be the easiest means of building up a connectian that should, by recommen lelious, geow,from year toyear. It weield seem that at last opinion has turned rgainq the osprey, for the majority ,df the mew mounts -are either wpm or those witfx Impeyan •pheasant tips, mounted on a whalebone stem. This is welcome news. Quills are, and will be egeeedinaly fashionable, especially those made up into large tuftsr•flussar fashion, or rising in pairs, out of outstretched wings. 'Many of the most up to date hats are .being trimmed with peacock's feathers andenwl's heads. The old super- stitione concerning .peacock's feathers being unlucky, seems to be fast dying out in this.matter of fact-age. Short boas of ostrich feathers, test crossed-at the throats or merely ruffle form, are now being-shown in nearly all the London shops, and already-sable tippets, minuskeads, but boasting many -Wife have reappeared. Persiad :amb is to enjoy great fevour this coming win- ter so E-hear upon the very test authority, .ateie also goldeneetter and ehincilla. The little short sevaisted eeueyee, are I notice, giving way tothe lenges-mode, which iceaches to the waist. The iceertion craze is still rampant, and lottg•exay it continue so. It lends itself to so 'many variations, ; Venetian. Irish, euipure with straight or scalloped edges may bescmployed. It can eitber be laid-on plain or over coloured ribbon, and arranged lengthwise, .slanting or across the bodice in any direction preferred. iThisi's an excellent method whereby to renovate abiouse for even- ing wear, that has also seen brighter daps. We harea, in recent times, had scares 'regarding many articles of food, mackerel, oysters,,potie,,milk,e&c., and it is coseiforting to find that their is absdiutely no ground for the `late rabbit scare. The number-of rabbits eaten in this country every year, is almost vlstbulouseand it would beta lamentable thing if any widespreaarpre- judice were engendered against a cheap and succulent article ofriood,hitherto justly considered as wholesome as it is sweet.

div.head: INSURING AGAINST WANT OF WORK.
div.p: INSURING AGAINST WANT OF WORK.

INTERESTING SWISS EXPERIMENT. A species ot insurance against the material Conse- quences of want of work is effected in England by many voluntary trade organisations. Owing in some measure to the failure in Switzerland of trade unionism and also to the remarkable development of State Slcialiam, that country is (says the" Times", endeavouring to compass the same end by the aid of legislative measures. Optional insurance against loss of work is offered to its settled labouring classes by the municipality of Berne ; Basle proposes to introduce an obligatory system shortly ; and compulsion is already in force in the town of St. Gall. The cantonal law on the subject came into operation in June. 1894. but St. Gall is the only town in the canton which has yet experimented with it. By virtue of this unique law the municipal council has established and itself manages, an industrial insurance fund to which all male ,wage-earners resident in St. Gall whose .average earnings do not exceed 51. daily are bound to belong, while better-paid workers can join or not as they please. Apprentices and labourers under age in receipt of less than 2f. daily are exempt while women may be allowed or required to join according to circumstances. Persons already belonging to a voluntary insurance organisation are relieved of ,the obligation to,join. The premiums are griduated as •follows::—A, where daily wages do not exceed 31. 153. B. where such wages do not exceed 41 20c.; and C, where they do not exceed sf. 303. The sums paid to those out of work class A, if. 303. per day; class B, 2f.'loc ; class C, 2f. 40c. This money has to bc ;fetched by the insured at the end of the week, though he must show hinvelf once a day. Relief is only granted 'for ten weeks (60 dayst) in any one year. and it is with- held altogether when the insured is without work owing to'fault,ofilis own •(this includes strikes), and when being able-bodied, he declines to accept work suited to his position and capacities when it is offered A. 'labour bureau is connected with the insur- ance fund. The working classes ot St. Gall have not in general taken kindly to this fatherly concern for their welfare, and cnmplianee with the law even now is understood to be not cheerful, but grudging. Evasion was anticipated by a provision which threatens with a •fine, and even in bad cases with imprisonment, such working men as neglect to pay their premiums after ;being once warned. With a revenue from premiums that is small when compared with the calls made upon it, especially in winter, the as urance fund has to rely to some extent upon auxiliary sources of income, the .chief being an annual municipal grant in aid.- During the first six months' operation of the insurance fund (July Ito December 31, 18954 3.430 persocs were regis- tered on the books, of whom 1,678 were married men and 1.666 single. . They renresentecl no fewer than 90 trades and occupations ; 2.41 E of them were in receipt of wages not exceeding 3f. a day; 920 received from 3f. to 4f.; only 98 received from V. to sf. By Jane of. the present year ,4,200 persons had been insured.. It remained to be added that the experiment will cense in 18. 97,unles tket;eitizens by prebiscite should decree its continuance in the,coming autumn.

MANCHESTER. SHIP CANAL COMPANY.
DIRECTORS' REPORT.

The report of the directors and statement of accounts for the half-year ended June 30. to be submitted to the shareholders of the Manchester Snip Canal Company at the meetins., held on Tuesday, were issued on Friday evening. The directors state that the expenditure on capital account daring the half-year, after deducting proceeds ef sales of land and plant was £52,757, making a total expenditure out of capital of £15,154,203 and leaving a balance on that Account of £250,132. The receipts on Ship Canal revenue account amounted to £81,214, and the expenditure including £36,701 for dredging and other maintenance, and £1,972 for ex- ceptionally heavy law expenses, to £88,643, leaving a debit balance of £7,429. The profits of the Bridgewater undertaking amounted to £22,566, leaving a balance of £15,137 carried to net revenue account, to which are added bank interest and surplus of realisation of cash invested in consols,amounting to £7,936. making a total credit on net revenue account of £23,073. The denit balance on net revenne account brought forward from last half-year was £79,212, which is increased by the addition of interest on mortgage debentures for the half-year viz :—L157,242. The total debit balance at the date of the account amounted to £213,382, but as the Corporation of Manchester have allowed their inter- est to remain in arrear there was an available balance of £67,888. Interest for the half-year on the first and second mortgage debentures, amounting to £44,742 has been paid, but the interest payable to the Manchester Corporation amounting to £112,500 remains in arrear, in addition to the interest due at the close of the previ- ous half-year, viz :—£168,750, making a total amount due, but not paid, to the Corporation of £281,250.

div.head: BRIEF HOLIDAY IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: A BRIEF HOLIDAY IN SCOTLAND.

Scotland had often been pointed out to me as a place for an ideal holiday. There, I was told, was to be seen the most romantic and picturesque scenery in the United Kingdom, and there I should find the climatic conditions healthful and invigorat- ing. With but one short week at my disposal it was, 3 f course, out of the question to attempt any- thing approaching a tour of the northern country, and accordingly the visit was restricted to the Clyde and the Western Highlands. At noon, just a fortnight ago, I found myself one of a party of five —which may be called a Warrington party—en- training at the Central Station for Liverpool from whence we were to sail in the "Pointer," one of the fine steamers belonging to Messrs. Burns and Company, to Glasgow. Those who do not tare for sailing such a long distance and who are apt to be troubled with mal-de•mer do far better and save considerable ti me by travelling direct by rail. But should the steamer Ns decided lupon for the journey, it is well worth while remembering that the bertha should be 'secured beforehand, or the tourist may find to his dismay that all the sleeping accommodation is occupied and he is compelled to pass the night on theopen deck. The time taken in the sea voyage to Glasgow is from fourteen to twenty hours, and to those unaccustomed to extensive sea trips the 'journey is found to be long and tedious. Rough sea is experienced after passing the Point of Ayre 'until Aliso Craig—a solitary rock abruptly jutting out in the. Firth of Clyde—is reached. 'Whilst lying in my berth I realised to some extent what kis to be "rocked in the cradle of the deep?' With the toss- ing of the vessel, the throbbing of the engines, the rankling of the steering gear, besides the conscious- ness of a fellow passenger in the same cabin being in distress, sleeping is at a discount, and one begins to feel a trifle uncomfortable. But next morn- ing these little inconveniences are soon forgotten in the thrill of delight which is experienced when sailing up the Firth of Clyde. Favoured with 'fine weather, the sight is certainlg a grand one. On tthe right, Ayrshire is to 159 seen in the distance, whilst near on the left, the mountainous isle of Arran with its rugged peaks presents a magnificent spectacle. Stilt steaming ahead ,Bute is reached,and a brief stoppage is made at Rothesay with its environment of hitls,pleaoantly situated in ttothesay Bay. A small sailing boat draws along- side the steamer and takes ashore the tourists who have decided to visit 113the8ay, and as we sail on- ward to the North,they give us three hearty cheers. Passing the entrance to the Kvqes of Bute and leaving Dunoon on the left, the mouth of the river Clyde is shortly entered. Greenock—a 'tiny hiv t of industry—is the next calling lace, and here a stay of over an hour is made. The 'remainder of the passage up the Clyde to Glasgow 'is not worth the time bestowed upon it unless the tourist has a strong desire to see the shipbuilding yards which are blustered along the banks. On Sunday morning, however, as we passed theca, tke clanging of the hammers was hushed, and our attenticn . _

Otheranunicipalities might with &silvan- -1 tave take a lesson from Glasgow which seems to 'be 'butFrn or t of a Chamberlain to sound her triumphs. 'But it was not. to a manufacturing city like 'Glasgow that we had come for change of air and rest and therefore the earliest opportunity was taken to make tratks for a more desirable holiday .place, titian was the place selert,A, which really is the capital of the West Highlands. It can be approached by the Caledonian Railway or by steam- boat. 'By the latter route—which is the more ,pnpular--you can ptoceed down the Clyde from 'Glasgow te Ardrishaite, thence through the Crinan Canal—a sort cut which saves the circuit of the Mull of tiantyre—and afterwards from Crinan, by •steamer again, to Oben.. The charms of this route, readers of the " Princess of Thule " will have found 4:lesioribed .for them by Ma*. The twenty hours sail to Glasgow had not put us—or to be more strictly correct the small party from Warrington-- in that frame of mind, attributed to Oliver Twist ' to "'beg for mote," so we determined to go by rail, end the iourney was one to be long remembered. To feast the eyes on the scenery of the Trossachs is an era in one's life. After passing Callender the railway winds along the moun- tain slopes. and sweet, scents are wafted from the heather-clothed steeps which stand in their solemn grandeur with their wreaths of mist and whose only o^cupants seem to he a few herds of sheep. Several fine loas—notehly Loch Earn, Loch Awe. and Loch Mire with their limpid waters Tend enchantment to the view. Oben is at, the ter- minus tnwndoelfiatiniets hraascebeheikne otodnthaint "tnh: line, tourist Highland," It certainly is an attractive little nmt and has net t!ral beauties all its own. The well- sheltered bay is edged by white louses, shc:pa, and hotels—there are some thirty or for, y hatc,ls in Oban—and these have as a • haekgrounti sloping and weli-wooded heights, whilst right in front. of the bay there is the island of Kerrara with its mountainous scenery. The bay itself has been a great factor in making Oban the important ship- ping port it is.On every week-dav,a good number of

steamers sail for varieua interesting places in Scot- land, and the tourist is thus provided with a splen- did centre in Oban. During the season, it is no uncommon sight to see a score of private yachts at anchor in a e bay, which together with the smaller craft, lend to the bay a striking appearance. One of the events of the year is Oban regatta. In fine weather, the town is gay and busy,but if rain falls it is the very reverse. Unlike other popular resorts, no places of entertain- ment are provided, and if the elements are against you, you must remain indoors or be prepared to face them. In the immediate vicinity of Oban there are many interesting places, both inland or down the coast. Within a short distance there are three historical castles around which are woven many historical associations, viz.; Dunollie, Dun- staffnage,and Gylen on the island of Kerrara. Lack of space forbids entering into any details concern- ing them,but it may be stated that the tamous Cor- onation Stone, now in Westminster Abbey, was carried off by Edward I. from Dunstaffnage, a place declared to have been the capital of the old Dalrid- ian Kings of Scotland up to 850. A delightful drive is that to the falls of Lora at the entrance to Loch Etive, and a shorter one is the circular drive round Glenshellach and Gallanach, very similar to the one round the Great Orme's Head. It would be im- possible here to make mention of the many pleasant outlets from Oban by steamer. Almost every place of interest on and near the coast where a safe landing can be effected is visited,and scenery wild and grand meets the eye at every turn. The writer has a vivid recollection of a sail to Fort William, at the entrance to the Caledonian Canal, and within a short distance of Ben Nevis. It was early morning, and as we steered northwards past the entrance to Loch Etive and through Loch Linnhe with hardly a ripple disturbing the blue waters, surrounded by towering heights lit up by the morning rays, the sight was an impressive one. There is nothing very striking or picturesque about Fort William, which is visited chiefly on ac- count of its nearness to Ben Nevis. To those de- sirous of a stiff climb or anxious to throw off any superfluous energy, the ascent of Ben Nevis should satisfy them-. It is, of course, as everyone knows the highest mountain in Great Britain and towers to a height of 4,406 feet. A fine day is reauired for the ascent or it will be simply a waste of time and energy. We were fortunate in this respect, and the three of us who succeeded in reaching the summit, considered our- selves well repaid for our exertions—and they were exertions—by the grand panoramic view which we were able to obtain over mountains, valleys and lochs for miles around. The route is a circuitous one, but the ascent is made less difficult by a good track laid and maintained by those connected with the Ben Nevis Observat cry who ask for a small consideration from the climbers to keep it in repair. This is paid at the "half-way house,"which,at least, speaks for the considerateness of those connected , with the Observatory, for long before this is reached there are many who, starting with the best inten- tions of reaching the misty top, are to be seen with their backs turned to the great Ben and making tracks for Fort William once more. The second half of the ascent—often through clouds of mist— is more difficult than the first, and alter thread- ling his way along the stony path, the sight of the Observatory at the summit comes as a welcome relief to the weary traveller. The telegraph office which is also to be found there is frequently used by visitors who reach it as a metals of communicating with the outside world from the highest point in the kingdom. The des- vent is not so easy as many would imagine, for be- 'fore the'plains below are reached the traveller gets a shaking which he would not care to experience often. Well tired out, we were glad to join the tourist steamer at Fort William, bound once more I for Oban. _ _

_ The holiday passed all too quickly, and we were loathe to leave the Capital of the Highlands for Glasgow, where we expected to get on board the Spaniel tor Liverpool. On arrival at Glasgow.how- ever, we were not a little surprised to find that the steamer had departed. We were 'fortunate enough to catch attain, and raced after the steamer te Greenock where we succeeded in getting on board. A calm and quick passage brought us to Liverpol, the only incident calling for remark being a slight accident to one of the female passengers. She was gazing over the side of the vessel when her hair became entangled in the revolving rope attached to the instrument for registering the number of knots traversed. The 'rope had gained a firm grip of the unfortunate lady's hair, and she was unable to extricate herself. There were cries for help, and she was eventually released from her perilous position by a consider- able tuft of her hair being cut off with a penknife by J. H.
