div.p: SHIP CANAL TRAFFIC.

The gross receipts from the Ship Canal .undertaking amounted to £81,214, an increase as compared with the carrrenonding six months of the previous year of £18,177. The weight of inerch‘ndise paving tolls which passed over the Ship Canal during the two periods was : _
Six months ending June 30th, 1896, June 30th, 1895. TONS. TONS. In Sea-going Craft ... 667,952 ... 480,784 In Barges ... ... 155,127 ... 119,316
Total—

The sea-going traffic to the development of which all I efforts are being specially directed, continues to increase. ' The development would be much more rapid if lines of steamers with frequent and regular sailings from the ports which ship cattle as well as grain and provisions in such large quantities for consumption in and around Manchester could be arranged for. Now that the com- modious lairages erected by the Corporation of Man- chester are complete, the Port is ready to deal with the cattle which form a large component part of the cargoes from both North and South American ports. The ex- penditure on Ship Canal revenue account during the half-year was £7,429 in excess of the receipts, because dredging and other full maintenance were for the first time charged to revenue. Law charges, mainly in con- nection with the Railway Rates cases, were also very heavy. The receipts during the first half of the year have always been smaller than during the second half. If the rate of increase for the current half-year should be in the same proportion as hitherto, the year's work- ing of the Ship Canal undertaking will as a whole just about clear all expenses, leaving the Bridgewatet net revenue intact. This was the estimate previously put forth and it is borne out by the result of the half-rear under review. The railway rates to and from the Man- cheater Docks have not yet been settled with the various railway companies. One test case (against the Midland Railway, but affecting the principle involved in dealing with all the railway companies) has been decided by the Railway Commissioners in the company's favour on all the points raised. The directors hope that the negotia- tions with the railway companies interested,which have since been re-opened, will result ins settlement that will place the port of Manchester on equal terms in every respect with competing ports and prevent further ex- pensive litigation.
BRIDGEWATER UNDERTAKING.
The net revenue from this undertaking was £22,566. against £18,239 during the same period last year, when the traffic was seriously interfered with by prolonged frost.
PARLIAMENTARt BI7SINESS

The Bill deposited in Parliament last session, which provided, amongst other things, for the closing of the tidal openings in the Ship Canal, has been pissed. The Acting Conservator of the River Mersey has approved the plans, and a contract for the closing of the openings has been let. This step is expected to considerably re- duce the 035 t of dredging in the Canal, and will render navigation more satisfactory.
ENGINEER-1S REPORT.

The following is the engineer's report as to the pro- gress of the works: "Dredging operations have been continued without intermission during the half year, the quantities of silt and sewage sludge deposited in the Canal (partly brought in from the backs in the Estuary and partly brought down by the rivers Irwell, Mersey, and Bollin) having been so large as to require the con- stant employment of six dredgers and two grabs for the maintenance of the depth of water. The works for the permanent electric lighting at the docks have been com- pleted, and are in operation. 'The new hydraulic instal- lation at Mode Wheel has also been completed, and is at work. The thirteen warehouses which have been erected by the Manchester Ship Canal Warehousing Company Limited on the quays adjacent to No. 8 Dock are prac- tically complete, and the seven adjacent to No. 6 Dock are sonearly complete as to be in use for:Traffic purposes. Four of the new hydraulic cranes ordered have been erected on the quay of No. 6 Dock. Some additions to and extensions of the railway system round the docks have been carried out. At Latchford Locks, the inter- mediate gates, which were carried away by the s.s. " Harold," have been re-constructed and replaced. The new steel gates, which are intended to replace the upper gates temporarily, are practically finished and will , shortly be fixed in position. The deep water jetties and 1 coal tip at Runcorn have been completed and are in use. The side dock for the reception of the pontoon at Elles- mere Port has been completed, and the dredging of the dam in front thereof is in hand. The slopes of the canal generally are in good condition. The works throughout the canal have been efficiently maintained, and are in good order. MEETING OF SHAREHOLDERS.

The half-yearly meeting of the shareh .Iders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held on Tuesday. Mr. Bythel, the chairman of the company, in reference to the financial position eulogised the Manchester Cor- poration for their liberality in not taking irterest on their advances in order that the working of the canal might not be embarrassed. The dredging ot the water- way and the removal of sewage entailed a great expen- diture. There seemed to be abselutely no mitigation of the evil, the deposits in the canal being as great as ever. As the traffic developed the necessity for raising new capital must be faced, and the directors were consider- ing how this should be done.. Ile traced the history of the negotiations with the railway co-opanies, and inti- mated that in all probability the question of through rates would have to be fought out before the Railway Commissions. The chairman alsa stated that a power- ful company was about to be formed for the creation of a" Manchester fleet " of steamers adapted to the canal traffic. The report of the directors was adopted with only one dissentient.

.c..-h THE statement of affairs vihiriv was submitted to the half-lea' " meeting of the shareholders of thsf Ship Canal Cbmpany on Tuesday was not withon its hopeful features, but at the same time it not be considered exhilarating reading by the!: who are interested, financially or otherwise, in t.bio canal. The canal still falls far short of paying 16 own way. The receipts from traffic during 04. first six months of this year amount to £81,216 This is £18,17.7 more than was received in thi.o first half of last year, but it still falls short of tP, working expenditure by £7,,,429,. In addition t' the working expenditure there is, of course, thet interest on the immense amount of capital We°, upon the canal, and towards the- payment of capital nothing is provided by the income from r:A fic. If the original shareholders, who subset:o'i something like ,000,000, be left out of accouen altogether,the corapany is still under an obligati% to pay interest upon the first and second mortgegt debentures and on the large loan of the Maneheststi.o Corporation. It may, therefore, be asked, hog' view of the fact that the income does not evei cover the-working expenditure, the interest °be these debentures 'and loans- is to be met. / answer is,that the interest on the Manchest4,o Corporation loans is not being paid at all, obi t the interest on the debentures is being paid Otio of capital. The interest upon the Corpor9ti°o loans for the half-year amounts to no less aOa than £112,600, and this together with what 13° become previously due already makes a total (io £281,250. This sum of considerably more thae quarter of a million has not, it is needless to 011/1 been struck out of the books of the Canal ComPl It has.simp ly, in effect,,been transferred to coPla, account, and represents so much more indebtej ness to the Manchester Corporation. The Cial;, is, in, fact, rapidly becoming a municipal und.o taking. The Manchester Corporation has otb° become so deeply involved that it cannot draw even if there were the desire It has vancad its millions of pounds and there is no rof sent prospect of the redemptioi. of these lose even of the pa37ment of interest upon them. 90. year will probably see a further important s t the direction of municipalisation, for it is evidei:ll- from Mr. Brrnmaits-speech that more capital /fri, soon have to be raised. This capital is nec.005;0,. in order to provide for an increase of tO et More machinery,, more warehouses, and dock accommodation are needed and mustbe °rot plied if Manchester is to be made into a glip. port. Where is this capital tt-,- come from ? t BYTHELL throws out some hints that at leilstr. , portion of the additional appliances may be Ilse. vided by private enterprise, but it is -more tPtc„ probable that private speculators will prefaroli await further developments before risking ratio• or their money. On the other hand it ill' to practically impossible for the Canal Co1flP°1•1 Wbe raise more funds in the open market.. ie. therefore,, the Chairman of the Canal ConzP3llllie tintates that more capital is to be obtaineuber must almost of necessity mean that the Ifigic co dvsn ter Corporation is again to be asked to 3 aro* what is needful. The Corporation maypef 'ill to refuse to do anything of the kind but, for three reasons, it is hard‘y likely to do se. 00 first place the citizens of Manchester loogrprio the Canal as their own particular cote de, and they are trot yet prepared to acknowlecirs sed feat. There is still that other reason to which we have already referred which will weigh very heavily on the side of a new loan, namely, the fact that the Corporation is financially already so deeply implicated. THE British sailor is receiving tritiih Sailors.; an unusual amount of atten- tion at the present time, but if half of what is said be true.he deserves a good deal more consideration than he has yet received. This -country is spending some millions of pounds in order to turn out a mighty fleet of war vessels, but the most expensive and best-constructed war vessel is only a helpless hulk if it be not manned by brave and skilful seamen. The subject of the 'supply of British sailors was touched upon by Lord CIIARLES BERESFORD in the speech he made to the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce a few , Weeks ago, and he warned the country against the gradual eliminatic,n of British seamen by foreigners. This week a London newspaper, the "Westminster Gazette," has been getting further Information upon the subject from the representa- tives of both the sailers and the shipowners. Both Sides agree that "Jack Tar" is having a bad time of it just now, and neither seems to be very hope- ful of finding a remedy. According to an official of the Seamen's Union, shipowners do not display any patriotic preference for the seamen of their own nationality. They are perfectly cosmopolitan in their employment of labour, and the result .s a wholesale expulsion of Brit ish sailors and firemen from British ships. The official re- ferredto estimates that since the formation of the Shipping Federation no fewer than eighteen thou- sand British have been displaced in the mercantile marine by foreigners of divers nationality. As might be expected when once the system had been adopted, the evil is rapidly spreading. Shipping eornpanies which at one time would not look at foreigners are now prepared to employ anything Which comes cheapest—Lascars, Chinese or Japan- ese. Under these circumstances the "Jolly Jack Tar" is almost bound to go to the wall. He can- not be expected to compete on the score of cheap- ness with Lascars and Chinamen, nor will he ever submit to the treatment which these Orientals take as a matter of course. Mr. G. A. LAWS, the general manager of the Shipping Federation, evi- dently takes his stand upon the ground that ship- owners are perfectly justified in buying their labour in the cheapest market, irrespective of nationality. E the true-born Briton will not take the pay that is accepted by the Dutchman, the Scandinavian, or the Chinaman lot him stand down in favour of the alien. Should the British seamen organise a strike, Mr. Liws predicts that it will be all the worse for themselves. "Plenty of foreigners" he says," will be found ready to take the place of those who refuse to work." This may be all right from the point of view of the shipowner whose objectis profit, but what is te be said about it when viewed from the national standpoint. Foreign seamen will be useless for manning the war vessels which are being turned out so rapidly from the shipyards of the country. A. great deal has been said recently about the need for more ships, but, already, in the opinion of not a few competent observers the most import- ant question is the one of" manning the Navy:,

This week's licensing sessions, though the chief item of interest in Runcorn, proved but a tame affair after all. None of the licenses were the sub- ject of objection or contention and they were all renewed as they stood. One application was made tor an off-license for Balfour-street but in common *Rh the magistrates throughout the country when dealing with fresh applications, the local bench Would have none of it. At present there are 44 licensed victuallers, 53 bear sellers and 5 others who sell off the premises in the Runcorn Division,so that the trade—the great trade —is fairly well repre- sented in the town.

The conduct of the license-holders in the divi- sion may be said to be good, as only two licensed Victuallers and two beersellers have been proceeded against during the year and one beerseller son- victed. In the prosecution for drunkenness 121 Was the number proceeded against, and out of that number 119 were convicted, as compared with 111 and 101 respectively last :year. This is a slight in- crease but it is as favourable as the present system of drinking will allow.

While on the subject of drink a reference to the presecution of sailors for drunkenness recently, might very well be made. It was given in police evidence that sailors coming to the town get drunk, and proceed straightway in that condition to their ships. It was even further stated that if inexor- able time prevented the sailors from getting drunk in the public-houses they laid in a supply to drink on the way back to ensure their incapability of taking care of themselves. This is a pity, because the canal banks at nightfall are only safe for sober people:to traverse as will be amply borne out by the fatalities reported in the " Examiner " a few Weeks ago, directly traceable to drink.

We bear that Mr. Robert A. Foulkes, of Prod- sham, is about to sever his connection with the Camden Soap Works, Runcorn, a firm with which he has been connected for upwards of 30 years. Latterly as a traveller, Mr. Foulkes has be come well-known to the tralezmen of Runcorn veso, ac- cording to a circular bearing Mr. Joseph Pritchard's nap:lB as secretary, are" taking this fitting oppor- tunity to make him a suitable acknowledgement of his long association with the trade in the! town." It is a worthy object well deserved, by virtue of Mr. Foulkes' 30 years of service.

The real effects of the Agricultural Rating Bill will soon be thorou4hly understood by the rate- Piyers of the country and the taxpayers of the town. The central government is now gathering the necessary information so that it may know exactly how much it will have to rob urban Peter 'of in order to pay rural Paul. At the Warrington Highway Board meeting the Clerk explained how the highway rate would be affected by the tew Bill. The highway rate is one which rural residents and especially those connected with the land get the full benefit of, yet they are to be re- lieved of a considerable part of it. If we suppose 'that at the present time £l,OOO is raised weans of that rate from agricultural land around Warringtom, when the Bill comes into t)Peration the rate will at once be reduced by one half. In other words the Highway Board will only teceive £5OO. It is needless to say that the expen- diture of the Board will not be red ueed by half. It will still spend the full £l,OOO, the missing .£5OO ,hz'ing replaced by an equal amount which will be -alcen from the general taxes of the country. As these taxes are for the most part paid by towns- People, it will be seen at once what a large subsidy !'he Government has given to the landed class. It " a long time since this country saw such a stupendous piece of political bribery as that effected by the Agricultural Rating Bill.

div.head: RTINCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RTINCORN AND WIDNES.

LOCAL SUCCESS. At the Cheshire Agricultural Society's Show at Chester held this week, Mr. J. H. Weston, of Runcorn secured second place with his beautiful St. Bernard " Sir Visto," against a remarkably good class of entries. r-r.NRO PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, RUNCORN. On Wednesday afternoon the members of the Bee Hive Sewing Class, belonging to the above place of worship, had their annual pic-nic, tm Rock Savage. Tea was served during the afternoon, by Miss Flaxworth who was in charge of the class. HALTON-ROAD WESLEYAN CHURCH RUNCORN. On Sunday next the annual choir sermons will be Preached in the Halton-road Wesleyan Church,Runcorn. Two sermons Will he preached by the Rev. W. Arrow- smith, formerly of Runcorn, and special music has been selected for the occasion by the choir. MARRIAGE Ot MISS L. HANDLEY, RUNCORN. An interesting marriage took place at the Bethesda Chapel OR Friday morning between Miss Lizzie Handley youngest daughter of Mr.Fla.ndley J.P.and Mrs.Handley, of Runcorn. The bridesmaid was Miss D. Cameron and Mr. H. Handley, officiated as best man. Both the par- ties are well-known in Runcorn, and as a result, con- siderable interest was taken in the wedding.
RUNCORN BRIDGE FARE.

The Highway Committee of the Runcorn Urban Dis- trict Council held a meeting on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. D. Bisbrowne. It was decided to recommend the Council to prepare a memorial to be sent to the L. and N.-W. Railway Company asking for a reduction of fares to pedestrians crossing the bridge at Runcorn. This is in accordance with the notice of motion given at the last meeting by the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi. THE CLOSING OF THE RUNCORN SHOOTING RANGE. On Friday last official notice was received through Colonel Bonen, of the Cheshire district by the officers of the Runcorn Companies of the 2nd Earl of Chester's Volunteer Regiment stating that the shooting range must be closed until further notice. The Runcorn Volunteers are endeavouring to get permission to use the range until the competition for the Volunteer Club's gold medal is finished.

div.head: THEFT OF AN APRON AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THEFT OF AN APRON AT RUNCORN.

On Thurgday morning before Messrs. P. Speakman and F. J. Norman, at the Runcorn Police Court, Julia Colburn, a married woman of Cooper-sf. was charged with stealing an apron valued at Gd. the property of Sophia Williamson of Thomas-st., on the 25th inst.— Mrs. Williamson stated that on Tuesday afternoon she went out leaving a son aged 11 in the house. Prisoner went to the house during hcr absence and asked the boy for an apron which she said his mother had given her. She looked about and found the apron (produced) which she took with her. She was apprehended the same afternoon on a charge of drunkenness and the apron was then in her possession.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.

On Sunday evening after the service at St. Edward's Catholic Church, Runcorn, the members of the League of the Cross and the Children of Mary held a meeting in the rooms of the former society. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi presided, and made a presentation consisting of a valu- able prayer book, rosary beads in silver and pearl and a cashbox to Miss Mary Dickenson, who is leaving the town. Dr. Goatsldi referred to the valuable work Miss Dickinson had done during her 3i years stay in the town and also of the kindness she had shown to the Children of Mary during her period of presidency. They were exceedingly sorry to lose her services but she carried with her their best wishes for her future prosperity. Several members of the church also spoke in praise of Miss Dickesson's service to the church, and Miss Dickan- son briefly but suitably responded.

div.head: RUNCORN PRIZR CHOIR.
div.p: RUNCORN PRIZR CHOIR.

The annual general meeting of the Runcorn Tonic Sol- fa Prize Choir took place on Monday evening in the Ellesmere—greet schoolroom, the chair being taked by Mr. Wesley Co3ke. The financial statement showed that the year commenced with a balance of £1 10s. lid., and the receipts were prize money. Manehester £5, donations £45, entrance fees £lO Bs. 61, receipts ballad concert £l5 93. 6d., " Messiah " concert £l3 93. 8 i.o.nd " Joshua " concert £l9 183. 2i., total £ll2 63. 10d. The expenditure included Manchester competition £4 Bs. Bid., general accounts £3 173., ballad concert £24 is., " Messiah" £4l is. 31, and " Joshua" £47 17s. 40., total £l2l 53. 4d., leaving a deficit of £8 18s. 6d. The Secretary having read a very satisfactory report the following officers were elected : Mr. F. J. Normtn, J.P. (president), Mr. Holford (con- ductor), Mr. Willi tm Coventry (treasurer), Me4srs. Newell, A. Unsworth and G. W. Yates (co-secretaries), Mr. W. Pritchard (librarian). The committee is as follows :—Mr. Hughes (chairman), Misses Edwards, Hayes, Pope, and Mrs. Burrows (sopranos), Mrs. Stubbs, Mrs. Coventry, Miss Williams and Miss Harrop (con- traltos), Messrs. Wesley Cooke, T. Parry,J. Norbury and F. Corker (tenors), Messrs. Leath wood, Burrows, Harri- son and Shaw (bass).
INTERESTING WEDDING AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday afternoon a wedding took place, the contracting parties being Miss Frances Mary Sproston of Long Island city, New York, (eldest daughter of Mr. J. Sproston), and Mr. James Greenhalgh of Bolton. The ceremony took place in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, which was well filled by friends and relatives of the parties. The bride was given away by her uncle Mr. Morris, and the marriage service was performed by the Rev. T. Brackenbury, assisted by Rev. J. D. Brinford- Jones of South Devon. The bride wore a skirt of cream cashmere,with bengaline bodice, to match,trimmed with tulle and orange blossoms. She also wore a veil and carried a bouquet—the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids Miss M. Sproston (sister of the bride), and Miss H. Jones (cousin), wore heliotrope crepon dresses, trimmed with lace, whil6 the three other bridesmaids, Miss M. Greenhalgh (sister of the bridegroom), Miss M. Ward (cousin of the bride), and Miss E. Greenhalgh (sister of the bridegroom) were attired in dresses of cream crepon,trimmed with gold,and wore picture hats to: match. The wedding party eassembled at "Hill- side," Weston, the residence of the bride's uncle, and after the ceremony luncheon was served in a marquee in the grounds. The honeymoon is being spent at Windermere for which place the happy couple departed on Wednesday evening. The following are a list of the guests, Mr. W. Green- halgh (Bolton), Mr. A. Morris (Manchester), Mr. J. Winkley (Bolton), Mr. Darby (Bolton), groom.smen. Mr. and Mrs. Greenhalgh sen., Mrs. Morris, Mr. S. Greenhalgh, Miss Gregson, Mr. and Mrs. Nicholson (Bolton), Mr. and Mrs. Sutton (Birkenhead), Mr. and Mrs. Craddock, Miss Jones, Misses Ada,and Lilly Morris, Mr. C. Ward.

div.head: RUNCORN PARISH – 0110 RCH SUNDAY
div.p: RUNCORN PARISH - 0110 RCH SUNDAY
SCHOOLS' TRIP.

This annual excursion took place on Wednesday after noon and though the unfavourable state of the weathe in the morning kept many away who would otherwise have gone, about 700 scholars aud friends assembled and went by special train at eno o'clock to Frodsham. In charge of the party were the Revs. H. B. Firth and W. Scholes, together with the superintendent and teachers in connection with the schools. On arrival at Frodsham, Mersey View pleasure grounds were taken possession of, and as the weather had cleared up,the programme which was very elaborate, was carried out and thoroughly en. joyed. The greater part of the afternoon was taken up in sports, athletic and otherwise, arranged for the juveniles, and the eleven events were warmly contested and afforded amusement for competitors and spectators alike. The results were as follows : Boys' race, 6to 2 years, 120 yards: J. Boyle, Ist ; W. Davidson, 2nd; B. Hilton, 3rd. Girls' race. 120 yards, 6to 8 years : Eleanor Rhodes, Ist ; A. M. White, aid ; and Lizzie Holmes, 3rd. Boys' 1W yards race, 9to 11 years: Walter Maybue, Ist; Leonard Waterson, 2nd ; Leonard Whitfield, 3rd. 1 Girls' race, 9to 11 years of age, 120 yards : Louisa Tarlton, Ist ; Louisa Cropper, 2nd ; Vara Buxton, 3rd. Boys' race. 12 to 14, 120 yards : Albert Woods, Ist ; Edwin Harrison, 2nd; 'Thomas Hilditch, 3rd. Potato race for boys of 12 to 14 years : George Nicholls, let; A. Yates, 2nd; Albert Woods, 3rd ; Thos. Hilditch, 4th. Girls' race. 6to 8 years (thread the needle) : Eleanor Rhodes, Ist ; Lily Richardson, 2nd; Lily Woods, 3rd. Egg and spoon race for boys: Joseph Williamson, Ist ; George Geddes, 2nd : Arthur Yates, 3rd. Egg and spoon race for girls: Maude Owen, Ist ; Dora Boyers, 2nd ; Nellie Holmes, 3rd. Boys' wheelbarrow race, 10 to 14 years: Albert Woods, Ist, ; Edward Newton, 2nd; George Geddes, 3rd ; E. Chenery, 4th; Reginald Cooper, sth; and Arthur Yates, 6th. Sack race, for boys 12 to 16 yearr : George Geddes, Ist ; T. Wood, 2nd ; J. Harrison, 3rd. The following officials arranged the sports, success- fully : Handicappers, Messrs. A. Jordan and John Littler ; starter, Rev. H. B. Firth ; judges, Rev. W. Scholes,and Messrs. W. E. Dudley and E. Key; stewards, Messrs. Clare, Boyers, Dudley, Frankland, Gibson,Tonks, Hulme and Price. At tbe close of the sports the prizes were distributed to the successful competitors by Mrs. Kaye. Tea was served during the afternoon, and a re- turn was started at 7.15. The committee express satis- faction viith the local railway authorities who got the special trains safely and expeditiously away at both stations.

div.head: W ESTON.
div.p: W ESTON.

CHOIR TRlP.—Weston Church choir boys travelled to Southport on Tuesday by way of enjoying their annual outing. There was a muster of about 25 or 30, who under the care of the Rev. W. H. Staples had a capital day by the sea. The weather was not so favourable as might have been desired, though the afternoon wa, qulte tine. Runcorn was reached about 10.30.
Special detective duty is stated to have been ordered by the constabulary authorities at Dublin Castle owing to the discovery at a secret society of Ribboumen in Armagh.

div.head: UTE EXAMINER SATURPAY, AUGUST 29 1896.
div.p: UTE EXAMINER SATURPAY, AUGUST 29 1896.
BREWSTER SESSIONS.
RUNCORN.

The annual Licensing Sessions were held on Monday morning in the P.Thce Court, Runcorn, and great interest was taken in the proceedings and the seating and stand- ing accommodation of the Court was crovfdrd. The magistratfis on the bench were Messrs. J. Brumdrit, Henry R-cnol&, P. Speakman, James flaniiley, T. Rigby, J. W. Lighthurn and F. J.,Norman.

div.head: SUPERINTENDENTS REPORT.
div.p: THE SUPERINTENDENTS REPORT.

Superintendent °Well, in his report or. the conduct of licensed victuallers and beer retailers in the division during the past year, said there was 44 licensed victual- lers, 53 beer-sell.lrs, and 5 others who sold off the prem- ises, making a total uf 104, and giving an average of 249 of the population to each license. Two licensed victual- lers had been prosecuted during the year, one of whom was convicted, that bring an increase of one prosecuted and none convicted in the previous year. Two beer- sellers were proceeded agahist and none convicted,being an increwe of one proceeded against and none convicted in the preceding year. For drunkenness during the yeer 121 persons were preceeded against, 119 being con- victed, as comas red eith 111 persons proceeded aeaire:t last veer, and ICO cenvicted. Toere was ail increase of 10 pPrsons proceeded ageins-, for drenkeneess and 19 persons convicted when compared with last year. Two new lie rises were being applied for. Mr. Parting- ton's appßcation ime ohj-cted to, as he considered there were sufficient facilities in the neielib..orhood for obtain- ing beth beer and wine. The publican proceeded against was Joe ph Smith, of the " Dike of ‘Vellineton," Per- cival Lyle, who was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk on his own premises and £2 aed costs for permitting drunkenness on the 24:h December, 1895. Smith was also charged with being drunk on his own premises on 28r,11 December, 1895, and he was ordered to pay 34. 61. costs. Smith appealed to the Quarter Sessions against, the conviction for permitting drunkenness but the coil- viction Was confirtned.—The Cheirirran si i there was very little that could tie said abut the report presented by Superintendent Okell. There was just a little ha- crease in the number of publicans prosecuted, and per- haps that would be a warning to them to keep their houses in better condition next year. One license had been endorsed and the landlord appealed to the Q earter Sessions but the magistrates decision was confirmed. As the landlord was dismissed, and a new tenant put in the police had no objection to the renewal of the license nor to the renewal of the old licenses so that they would be all again renewed.
TRANSFERS.

The following licenses were transferred ;—Lowlands liotol, Lowland -road, from JnMPS C. Wylie to Thos. Houghton ; Anchor Inn. Brunswick-street, from Harry Arnold to Luke Holmes ; Bull's Head, Halton 11 from William Powell to Thos. Robinson ; Three Crowns, King-street, from Walter White to James Robinson ; Cornwall and Devonshire Arms, Church-street, from James Woodrow to Henry Moxton ; Village Inn, Halton from Th,.s. Molyneaux to George H. Andrew's ; Volun- teer Inn, Granville-street,froin John Sadler to Joseph E. Jones ; Vine Hotel. Lowlands-road from Peter Hadley to Thomas J. Sloane.—The transfer of the license of the Oddfellowe Arms to Albert Grillitos was held over, as the applicant did not appear.

div.head: APPLICATION FOR A WINE LICENSE
div.p: APPLICATION FOR A WINE LICENSE

Mr. Linaker applied on behalf of John H. Weston for premises situate in Devonshire Square, Runcorn.—The applicant Mr. Weston stated that he was a chemist and druggist and he was applying for a license for the sale of wine en his premises in Devonshire Square under the Act of 1869 70. The rent he paid for the premises before he bought them was £45 pr year bat the place was his own property. The applicant with Charles Wright and William Webb proved that the usual formalities such as posting notices and advertising had been complied with.
APPLICATION poll AN OF! LICENSE.

George Pal tington applied bra wine and beer license i 3 Ballour-streetßuncorn.—Mr. A. Browne. of Warring- ton on behalf of the applicant said the application was not only for a wine license but for power to sell beer off the premises which were situate in Balfour-road. With regard to the wine license, if he proves the usual condi- tions had been carried out, the bench had no power to refuse it so that the only question was whether they would grant a beer license for the shop. Higher Run- ' corn seemed to him to be a part of the town entirely away from Runcorn. It migtt be said that there were already sufficient beerhouses in the town to satisfy the people. Well,that might be so in the town but he con- sidered that the district was not adequately provided. There were 476 parochial electors in the district and if they gave an average of three or four grown up persons in each house that would mean something like 1200 liv- ina in the immediate neighbourhood. In the district there was Pimply one licensed house—" The Travellers' Rest "—and that was on a high embankment and was a house that was licensed for consumption on the pre- mises. There was a number of people who objected to sending their servants to a beerhouse or public-house but these would have no objection to sending to a shop where a business was already conducted,Mr. Partington was a man who had been in Runcorn 12 years and there ' was nothing against his character. His business was highly respectable and as he went round to numerous places outside he had been requested to supply beer in conjunction with other goods. His client did not intend to make the house a fully eut-loor licensed house. He was quite content to supply all that was re- quired in six days and they could if they liked put a clause to that effect on the license. His client did not intend to keep open until the limit allowed by licence but intended to close his shop at the usual time which was between 8 aed 9 o'clock in the week and 18.30 on E. turday nights. If local option had come into force in the district the voters would have the right to say whether the license was required or not and they the magistrates had thatzight. He asked, there- fore, as there was not sufficient recommendation that they would grant the license on the conditions named. The house was a good house, and was rated at £2l nett, and this was more than sufficient to cover the actual value as set down in the Act of 1869.—Mr. Partington was called and stated that he had been in Runcorn 12 years. There were 476 parochial voters on the last parochial list and there was no license in the Heath Ward, excepting the" Travellers' Rest," which was 480 yards from his house. He only wanted a sit days license, and he did not intend to keep open uotil 11 o'clock every night.—Mr.Oxworth:proved that he put up the required notice on the Parish Church door. -W.E. Lancaster proved that the names on an extensively signed petition in support of the licence were signed in his presence with the exception of a few which the applicant had pro- cured.—For the police, Sergeant Lee stated that he had measured the distances to the various licensed places, from the applicant's shop. To the Lion Hotel it was 373 yards, to the Traveller's Rest 462 yards, to Mr. Hill's beer-house 454 yards, to the Railway Hotel 574 yards. to the Swan lon 635 yards and to the Camden Hotel 639 yards.—Mr. Browne: We might as well have the' Wilson's Hotel measurement.—Sergeant Lee: If you had asked me I would have measured it for you.—Superin- tendent Okell : Do you think there is any necessity for the house ?—Sergeant Lee : Not the slightest—Super- intendent Okell : Are you aware that a number of the publicans in the town are living rent free P—Sergeant Lee: Tnere are one or two, sir.—Mr. Browne . How leng have you been in Runcorn P—Sergeane Lee: Nearly three years.—Mr. Browns: And do you put your opinion against older residents who have signed the petition.—Sergeant Lee: It is my opinion. There arc enough houses in the town already. Mr. Browne: That is in the centre of the town you mean. Sergeant Lee: All over the town. Mr. Browne: I suppose you object because you are instructed to ob- ject. Sergeant Lee: No sir, I have told you my opinion. DECISION Or TNE MAGISTRATES.
The magistrates retired for a lengthy period, and on their return the Chairman briefly announced that Mr. Vireston's license to sell wine was granted. The applica- tion of Mr. Partington was refused.

div.head: DARESBURY DIVISION.
div.p: DARESBURY DIVISION.
At Dareshury Court House on Tuesday before Mr. J. C. Parr (chairman), Mr. W. Long, Mr. C. H. Broadbent, Captain Rodgers, and Mr. H. Tinsley. TEE POLICE REPORT.

Superintendent Okell submitted his annual report with reference to the conduct of licensed victuallers and beer retailers in this division during the past year. Be said" there are 24 licensed victuallerstone beerseller,and four others who sell off the premises,total 29 ; giving an average of 326 of the population to each license. One licensed victualler has been proceeded against during the year but he was not convicted, being the same number proceeded against during lagt year and a decrease of one convicted in the same year. One beerseller has been proceeded against and not convicted, being an in- crease of one proceeded against and none convicted in the preceding year. Thirty persons have been proceeded against for drunkenness during the year, 29 of whom were convicted as compared with 26 per- sons proceeded against and 24 convicted during the pre- ceding year. There is thus an increase of tour persons proceded against and five persons convicted. One n3w license is being applied for at Grappenhall which I object to, as I consider there are at present sufficient facilities for obtaining refreshments, etc., in the neigh- bourhood."
Mr. Parr remarked that it seemed to be a normal con- dition of things. There was nothing for congratulation )r the reverse.
The Clerk: Are there any objectims to the present existing licenses in the Division of Daresbury. SUperintendent Okell : I have none.
A PROPOSED LATCFIFORD LOCKS HOTEL. THE LICENCE REFUSED.

Mr. A.Browne said he had to apply on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., for a new license at Latch- ford Locks on phe new Thelwall road between Latchford and Thelwall. Their worships were aware that when the Ship Canal was made it entirely altered the natural divisions of the county. A further alteration was caused by the new Warrington Borough Extension Act, by bringing the boundary up to the canal. The application he was making was for a very handsome house to cost between two and three thousand pounds, with every

convenience including a bowling green. It was not for the purpose of GI appenhall alone—because he would be met by the Superintendent saying there were already two public houses which were sufficient for the nurnb2r of inhabitants—but lie was applying on th,- ground that a large number of persons came to the locks on business. more e-pecally in connection with the steamers. He •was going to prove tat on a number of oe,casious they had lying up at Latchford several vessels winch had to remain at the Locks during the night. Whilst there toe men on board, who had perhaps boen at s,:a two or three weeks, wanted some recreation and he suggested that there is as no harm whatever in their having a game of billiards at this hotel, which would be conducted on the strictest principles for supplying drink and food. The magis- trates would know that steamers were thus obliged, sometimes to wait at Latchford all night, and not only steamers, but people had sometimes to wait three or four hours for a steamer to come from or go to Manches- ter. In that case they had nowhere to go except to the " Dog and Dart," a mile away ; or the Cheshire Cheese, 1200yds away, and in the meantime they might miss their boat alessrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., pro- posed to remove the evil by patting up a respectable house., not for the inhabitants of Grappenhall, but for the neighbourhood of the Locks, the Ship Canal having made an entirely different condition of things to what formerly existed. Another point was that the nearest public hoiqe was, as he had said, the " Dog and Dart " and that was 1,025yds away; the next was the" Railway Inn," Knutsford-road, 1,125 yards ; the " Ram's Head," 1,625 yards ; the " Barry Arms," 1,670 yards away ; and the " Pickering Arms," Thetwall, 1875 yards away. Of course there was the " Railway Inn," but that was in the Borough. The Superintendent had properly said on Monday that if they could make certain arrangements he would not ap- pose the license. They could not make those arrange- ments and the Superintendent was therefore bound to oppose the license. • He (Mr. Browne) asserted that there was no other opposition at all. Wny had Messrs. Green. all, Whitley and Co., intended to build this hotel ? For the simple reason that they had been requested to do so by a number of persons. There was at present no room for public meeting in the Parish. The Latchford Parish Council had no meeting place and in order to comply with the request of the members Mr. Owen had planned a room suitable for any meetings which might be necessary. There was a wish amongst certain gentlemen in Latchford to form a Masonic Lodge and they were wishful to use the room which would be provided. As time went on the traffic on the Canal would increase, and the road on which it was proposed to erect this hotel was the main road to Lymm, Altrin- chain and Manchester. A large traffic went past and their worships must take that into consideration. He understood that Mr. W. Owen, the architect, had, in the plans, set back the house some distance so that no traps or ether vehicles would obstruct the road. Mr. William Owen said he had been instructed to pre- pare plans for the proposed Latchford Locks Hotel. He bore out the facts of Mr. Browne's statement, and added that the building would be set back 20 feet from the road to allow carts, kc., to draw up on the premises. A good bowling green, gardens, and stables had been pro- vided for. The plans were then handed up to the magistrates who inspected them. Mr. John Lee, Birch Cottage, Latchford, said he was a member of the Latchford Parish Council. They had no meeting-house and had arranged to use this place if erected. He had lived in the district about 30 years. At the Locks he had seen a number of people waiting for hours. In his opinion the public-house was neces- sary. Since the road bad been diverted it was much more used. Mr. F. R. Roberts said he oppesed the application. He represented various ratepayers and had with him a memorial signed by them, and protesting against the license being given. To satisfy Mr. Browne he gave several names and added that most of the memorialists lived within a stone's throw of the Locks. They were in the township of Grappenhall. On the same side of the canal as the proposed site there was a row of cottages, and all the tenants of those catages had signed the memorial. Mr. Lee, cross-examined by Mr. Roberts. said that the Latchford Parish Council had met on every occasion necessary. They had not had to meet in the open air. They had met without inconvenience. The circum- stances Mr. Browne had alluded to would apply on Latchford Without going into the borough. At the present time they met in the Baptist schoolroom. Mr. Roberts : You don't meet in the Parish of Latch- ford Without P—Witness : We do. Mr. Roberts: Then you have a meeting place 2 Witness: Yes. This portion will go into the horough. Mr. Roberts : Will you not have a meeting place then ? Witness : I cannot answer questions of law. Mr. Roberts : You will admit that the inhabitants of Latchford on the Warrington side of the canal are amply provided with facilities for drink ?—Witness : Certainly. Mr. Roberts: Have you any idea as to the opinion of the residents on the other side of the canal P—Witness : Yes. Mr. Roberts: What is their general opinion P—Wit- ess : That they are in favour of it. Mr. Roberts; Would you be surprised to know that I have a memorial signed by nine-tenths of them op- posing it P—Witness : No. You can get memorials fM• anything. Mr. George Pilling, Acker's-lane, said he was clerk to the Latchford Parish Ceuncil. They would not have a place to meet in after the 9th of November. The pro- posed house was ju"t on the border of the two townships. At Latchford Leeks he had seen people waiting for steamers, as they had no other place to go to. He bad also seen workmen there. They had had to have their refreshments sent to them. Witness had also seen boats lying up at the locks. Their officers had nowhere to go. In his opinion the house was required. He had had a conversation with the owner of all the houses Mr. Roberts spoke about, and he was in favour of the pro- posed hotel. Mr. Roberts: You have power to build a meeting place for the Parish Council if necessary P—Witness : Yes.—Mr. Browne: At the rate of ad. in the £. Mr. Roberts: Is there anythine to prevent you meet- ing where you do at the present time ?—Witness: No. It is not accommodating though. Sometimes we have meetings there when they tare holding services and we have had to go into a very small vestry. Mr. Roberts: Do you think the general community is opposed to this pub lie-house P—Witness : No. Captain Waring, Latchford House, said that ships stopped at Latchford Locks during the night,sometimes as many as seven at once. The sailors had nowhere to go. There was a largo number of men working at the locks a short time ago and there was no place close at hand for them to go to. He thought the house was necessary but would not have had anything to do with it except for its providing accommodation, such as beds and dinners. Cross-examined: There were people from abroad , landed at Latchford every day. Many peoplo also came from Liverpool by train to take ship back. Mr. Roberts: How often has that happened ? Witness : Three or four times a week. Mr. Roberts: With regard to sailors having to lie up. From your experience of sailors is it a great trial for one to go 1000 yards for a drink ?—Witness : N. Mr. Roberts : Is it not a rule for ships to carry grog ? Witness: No. There is no allowance on board. Mr. Roberts : Fo a sailor has to be a teetotaller while he is on board P—Witness : Yes.—Mr. Roberts : He is all the better for it. Do not accidents happen to men returning to their ships P—Witness : Sad accidents occur at times. Mr. James Shaw, Springfield, Stockton Heath, a tim- ber mei chant, said he was the applicant for the license. He intended to keep the hausesupplied with proper food, refreshments and beds. It was his intention to reside on the premises with his family. He had had 25 years experience in the licensing trade. Mr. Clark said on behalf of the firm he was authorised to state that the plans would be adhered to. Superintendent Okell then said he objected to the license on the ground he had stated in his report and would put Sergeant Gosling in the box. Questioned by Mr. Browne he said if one public- house in Grappenhall was done away with he would net object. Ho knew the firm could not do away with one. He had not had complaints from officera about having to take bodies from the Canal to the" Dog and Dart." P.S. Gosling' said that the proposed public-house would be 846 yards from the " Dog and Dart." The nearest beer-house was 7E2 yards away, in Thelwall-lane. Mr. Browne: You do not dispute Mr. Owen's figures do you ? How did you measure it ? Sergeant Gosling : I measured it with a 66 foot tape in the middle of the high road. I don't think there is any necessity for the public-house at all. Mr. Browne: Do you put your opinion against Mr. Lee's and others P—Sergeant Gosling : Yes. Mr. Roberts in his speech for the opposition, said his friend had made out from his po'nt of view a very admirable case. From the speaker's point of view he had made out no case at all. It was not sufficient in these days to bring before the bench witnesses who were more or less interested in the granting of the appli- tion and he hoped the magistrates would agree with him that a great deal of consideration had to be given to popular opinion. It was true that so far popular opinion had not been able to secure its rights in the way of legislation but it would be useless to deny that the trend of feeling to-day was that in the matter of licenses, popular opinion ought to weigh heavily with the magistrates. There was a group of some 40 or 50 houses which might be said to surround the site of the proposed public-house and the tenants of these houses objected to it. It was all very well to say vessels up the canal might carry a fugitive passenger. They might have bona-fide travellers Moo wishine to rest and get a drink, sod it might be that a body had to be carried an inconvenient distance. To say nothing of the specious- ness of arguments of that kind they had a number of people who had to live in the immediate vicinity and had to endure all the noises, all the indecency and im- propriety cf conduct which characterised the fre- quenters of these places from a distance,but Mr. Browne had not said a word with regard to those people Iwho frequented the region of the Locks at Latchford, viz., colliers from Bedford Leigh,and other places, who came in wageonettes. Their visits were becoming a crying evil and an intolerable nuisauce.3lle might safely say

that with regard to those people most affected, and who had to endure that kind of thing,there was a unanimous aid deep feeling that if the license was granted it would .112 the lite in the district almost intolerable. He thought that seeing that the applicants had not voiced the feel- ing of the residents at all he could show that that feeling was unanimously against the granting of the license. The facilities for the obtainin_f of drinks were reasonable as a man by walking eight or nine hundre: yards could get all the drink he desired. Mr. Roberts thought the magistrates wou!cl be doiag a dangerous thing in planting a public- ii use on the bank of the Canal, as a man with more drink than was good for him,might easily fall in. He ai pealed to them to reject the application. The me- moriai upon which he laid most stress was from those inhabitants he had spoken of, who pratically all lived in thd parks of Grappenhall A large nurnper of the me- morialists too were employe 4 on toe Ship Canal. Alb .rt Hampton proved the signatures on ti•.e mem- orial which were made in his presence. At the request of Mr. Roberts he read the memorial to the magistrates. It said the memorialiits viewed with apprehension an application for a license to sell intoxicating liquors at Latchford Lleks as the present numoer ot houses was in excess of the requirements of the district. [hey pray, d the magistrates not to grant the application. Mr. Browne : I suppose you only canvassed teeto- tallers.
Witness: I canvassed drunkaras as well. (Laugh- er.) _ _
The magistrates retired and returning in about 10 minutes the e.hairman said he regretted to inform Mr. Browne thlt the magistrates were unanimous in refusing the application.
WARRENGTON. NEW APPLICATIONS REFUSED.

On Thursday morning the annual Brewster Sessions for Warringten were held in the Court House, Irlam et., before the following members of the Licensing Commit- tee :—The Mayor, Mr. F. Monks, Councillor Pierpoint, Mr. J. W. Hayward, Mr. E. J. Guest, and Mr. J. H. F:eming. There were also on the bench Messrs. T. Birchall, H. Roberts, Alderman Francomb, Calonel Ridg- waN , Alderman Sutton, and S. Wright. The legal gentlemen present were Mr. Segar, barris- ter, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. J. Longland), Mr. T. Swift, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. A. Browne), and Mr. F. R. Roberts, solicitor, Warrington. In the well of the Court there was a large attendance of spectators among whom were the Rev. E. T. Reed, Councillor Shaw, Councillor Rogers, Councilor Baird, Mr. R. Storey and Mr. S. B. Stringer.

div.head: ALEHOUSE AND MUSIC LICENSES.
div.p: ALEHOUSE AND MUSIC LICENSES.

The Chief Constable said there was no objection on the part of the police to any of the existing alehouse licenses. —These were all renewed.—. The Chief Constable then informed the magistrates that with regard to the music licenses there was also no objection. There had beeß no complaint during the year of any of thent.—All were renewed.

div.head: CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.
div.p: THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.

Mr. Luke Talbot, the Chief Constable presented his annual report which was accepted by the magistrates without 13-ing read. It was as follows:—Chief Constable's Office, Thursday, August 20th, 1896. To the Worshipful the Justices assembled at the annual licensing meeting of 1896. Gentlemen,—l have the honour to submit to you my first annual return relative to the business of this session. The number of licensed houses in the borough is as follows :—Licensed victuallers, 86 ; beerhouse keepers 45 ; off-licence holders. 75 ; total, 206. The popu- lation to each licence is 253.033. according to the census of 1891. During the year one licensed victualler, viz., Margaret Green, the "Shakespeare Inn," was convicted of supplying drink to drunken persons, and was fined : no other licence holder has been proceeded against. A tabulated form annexed shows that during the past twelve months 264 persons have been proceeded against for the offence of drunkenness, a decrease, lam happy to say, of 64 from the number prosecuted during the preceding year. Licenses have been transferred to twelve licensed victuallers, seven beerhouse keepers, and six off-beersellers, making a total of 25. The applications to be made at the present sessions are :—One by William Bolton, Esq., far a full license for the house which is at present an off-licensed beerhouse at the corner of Lord Nelson-A.. Howley ; the second by Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, for an ale- house licence for the premises known as " Orford Lodge, Orford-lane. ' • Applications will also be made for the renewal of all existing licences. Twenty-seven ale- houses. eight beerhouses, and eleven other public rooms (total 46) are licensed for music and dancing. They have during the year been generally well-con- ducted ; no professional musicians or vocalists are em- ployed in any of the alehouses or beerhouses. Tne man- ner in which the licensed houses have been conducted during the year has been on the whole satisfactory, and I observe with gratification an increasing care on the part of publfcans in the exclusion ef drunken persons from their houses, and generally in the maintenance of good order on their premises. In the following tables, No. 1 shows for the past ten years the number of licences existing within the borough, with the number of persons during each year proceeded against for licens- ing offences, or for the offence of drunkenness. Through the courtesy of several of my colleagues, I am enabled to give in table No. 2. for purposes of comparison, a return of prosecu ions for drunkenness during the past 12 months in many of the neighbouring towns. I have the honour to be, g.ntlemen, your obedient servant, LIMB TALBOT, chief constable." Table No. 1 showed that in the year 1827 there were 87 fully-licensed victuallers in the town, against 86 at the present time. Beer-house keepers numbered 48 in 1887 and 45 in 1896. and shon-keepers with licenses showed an increase from 71 in 1887 to 75 In 1896. The persons charged with drunkenness numbered as follows ;-1887, 568 ; 1288, 742 ; 1889, 793; 1890, 806 ; 1891, 773 ; 1892, 680 ; 1893, 606 ; 1894. 458 ; 1895, 328 ; 1896, 264. With regard to this year's figures it may be stated that the figures for drunkenness are between July 31st, 1895, and August let, 1896. We take the following from the second table alluded to : Name of Town Persons pro- Population Number ceeded against Census per 1 030 of 1891. population

Viazmngton ... 264 ... 52,743 ... 5•0O5 SUGGESTED NEW PUBLIC-HOUSE AT HOWLEY.—
ALDERMAN BOLTON'S APPLICATION.

Mr. Segar, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. J. Longland) apeeared on behalf of Alderman Bolton, and said he asked for a provisional full licence for the sale of intoxicating liquors at a house proposed to be built on the site of the present beer off-licensed house which was situated at the corner of Admiral-street and Lord Nelson-street. The nearest fully licensed house, he said, was the Bull's Head, 516 yards away, in Church-street. There was a large area therefore, covered with working- men's houses and not supplied by a fully-licensed house. The plans prepared by Mr. J. E. Wright, showed a house in every way suitable for the purpose. The accommo- dation for the public was adequate and the sanitary arrangements were as good as it was possible they could be made. Barrels would be taken into the public-house by a cellar opening into a yard. so that the pubiic pass- ing along the highway would not be incommoded by ropes, etc. The building was arranged internally so that a barman serving behind the bar could seo into , all the rooms intended for public accommodation. The whole of the ground floor was devoted to the use of the public, and the persons living at the house would reside on the first floor where the kitchens, bedrooms, etc., were. The yard could thus be made use of without anyone having to pass through the private part of the house. It would be occupied by Mr. Reed, the present tenant of the off-license, if their worships granted the license. fhe plans were then inspected by the magistrates and explained by Mr. Segar, who went on to say that there was no back-door and no means whatever of persons slipping in or out without the police having an oppor- tunity of seeing what was going on. The yard would simply be used for the bringing in of what goods might be required. Mr. Bolton having theught that perhaps vaults would be objectionable he had canned the plans to be presented to the Court in the alternative shape which showed that instead of having vaults it was intended to put a news room and a bar in the place occupied on the plans by the vaults. Mr. Bolton, the applicant for this provisional license, he said, was a brewer, well-knewn in the town and had been for a long time controlling a number of licensed houses and his administration of those houses had been simply excellent so far as War- rington was concerned. There had been no conviction or charge against any a his heuses. He thought the records of the town would bear that out and that it was not necessary to call witnesses on that point. Mr. Bol- ton was the person to whom a license ought to be granted as he had experience, hed a good character and was an able administrator of public-houses. In the dis- trict there were few public-houses, and the area included a population of some 2000, or 3,000 persons to whom a respectable licensed house would be a boon. The land belonged to Mr. Bolton and he was prepared to buy up the neighbouring property for stables if required. He would, of course, give up the off-license if the applica- tion he now made was acceded to. Alderman J. E. Wright, architect and surveyor, sup- , parted Mr. Segar's statements about the structure of the public-house as planned. The rental of the house, he added, would be £5O or £55 at the least. Within 500 yards there were no less than 400 workingmen's cottages and the nearest fully licensed house was 516 yards away. Mr. Monks: How far is the "General Wolfe" off? Alderman Wright: 616 yards. Mr. Monks: and" The Marquis of Granby ?" ' Alderman Wright, 530 yards, He then gave the die-

tances of other public houses in the district. Mr. F. R. Roberts said he opposed the application on behalf: of two ratepayers, Mr. William Dutton, Porter- street, and Mr. William Noods,Dutton-street,both in the near neighbourhood of the proposed public-house. Mr. Roberts : Have you measured the distance? Witness : not myself.. Mr. Roberts : I cnake the distance very much less,- 440 yards to the" Bull's Head." Witness: It was measured from the Ordnance map, which, as a rule, can be sworn by. Mr. Roberts : "Ai a rule!" There are exceptions then. How long would it take a person to travelathe distance. Witness : ter.)
It depends on the state he was in. (Laugh-

Mr. Roberts : Well whether he was drunk or sober, I take it it, would not be more than live minutes, and would that exhaust a man ? Witness : I don't know. Mr. Roberts : What is the chief drink of the working men of Warrington ? Witness : I suppose it is beer. . Mr. Roberts: Do you know then that there are six or seven off-licenses within a quarter of a mile and also three beer-houses ? Witness : I don't know. I have not taken any notice of off-licenses or beerhouses. Mr. Roberts : Do you think the le4itimate needs of the workingmen ale sufficiently met in that district ? Witness : No. Alderman William Bolton after giving evidence.in support of Mr. Segar's statement said he had been a brewer over 30 years. and curing that time he had been controlling a number of public-house. n Warrington itself, and there riad been no convictiu—. against his houses. Be was always very careful in the selection of his tenants. Mr. Roberts: Do you know that taking the popula- tion of Warrington as 54,000 that it amoants to one fully-licenseJ house to every 610 people,including R omen and children ? Witness : Yes. Mr. Roberts : Do you know that there are 206 liceused houses where a man can get drunk? Witness : Yes. Mr. Roberts: And that for every 255 people there is a place where drink is to be had : Witness : That has nothing to do with it at all. Mr. Rcberts : Just answer the questions please. Mr. egar (looking at Mr. Roberts' paper) : This is not quite right, he has left out '033. (Laughter.) Witness : I will admit it. Mr. Roberts : It really means 150 men for each place.

Mr. Roberts : How far is your residence from the brewery ? Witness : About a mile. Mr. Roberts: Is it a great irmonvenience to go home for-dinher ? Witness: Not very. Mr. Roberts : Is it necessary that a man should be nearer drink than his dinner? Witness: Sometimes a man wants a drink more. Mr. Seger said that since Mr. Roberts' figures were published in 1891 the inhabitants bad increased. rhe only important matter in the case was that there was no licensed hou e for 500 yards and more. Mr. Roz erts suggested that the other application should now be heard CD that both could be considered at once. This was agreed to and Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons case was heard.
COUNCILLOR HENRY ROBERTS J.P.,

div.head: AND THE ABBEY ARMS.
div.p: AND THE ABBEY ARMS.
A COMPLAINT.

At the Oakmere Licensing Sessions, on Monday. the Chairman (Mr. James Tomkinson, of Willington Hall). announced that a letter had been sent to the Chairman ef the Bench by Mr. H. Roberts, Warrington, complain- ing that the, writer and two friends had visited the Abbey Arms Hotel on the afternoon June 18th and had asked the landlord for tea. The landlord had refused to serve them on the geaund that there was not sufficiont bread in the house, except what was just sufficient for the wants of the household supper. The landlord had informed them that the division police had been there for drill on that day and owing to having had to provide them with refreshments there was no bread left. They (the visitors) had been directed to the Blue Cap, a house some two and a half miles away, but in their exhausted state it was too much for them to go so far. They had received barely civil treatment at the house, and he had moreover been told that other people had been treated in the same way. As a magistrate of the borough of Warrington, he protested against it, and he desired to bring the matter under the notice of the magistrates. Superintendent Johnson said be had had a letter from the Chief Constable calling attention to the matter, and in answer to the Bench he said there had been similar complaints made in regard to the house. Mr. A. Fletcher, who appeared for Mr. Wilson, the landlord of the house, said it was only fair that when parties came to the hotel, as the party in question had done, some intimation of the fact that they wanted tea should be given to the landlord beforehand. On that particular day the supply of bread had run short, owing to the visit of the police officers. He had been instructed to deny any charge of incivility.for Mr. Roberts and his friends had been treated just as civilly as other people had been treated. He (Mr. Fletcher) had visited the house frequently during the last 30 years and had al- ways been treated with civility, and he had never heard of anyone that had been treatel otherwise. The licence was then renewed, the Chairman express- ing the hope that there was some misunderstanding over the charge of incivility.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL,
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL,
SHIPMASTERS' GRIEVANCES AT RUNCORN
DOCKS. ALLEGED GRAVE DELAY.

On Wednesday morning a deputation of shipmasters and owners had an interview at Runcorn Town Hall with the trades council, with respect to the delay in dis- charging ships at Runcorn Dacks. Mr. P. Speakman, „Ty C.a.. presided, and the deputation was introduced by Captain Millar, of the Countess of Carrick. The deputation presented a memorial to the council, in which it was stated that despatch in the discharge and loading, of cargo was the essential condition upon which shipping could be profitably worked. and this despatch had not been given at Runcorn Docks during the past month. Without any reference to custom as to turn, the ships at the lay-by had been given preference over those in the docks ; and steamers had been brought into dock, had been discharged and reloaded and sent away in the course of two days, while schooners that had traded to Runcorn for a quarter of a century and upwards had been lying idle in the Mersey and in the docks for at least a month. The delay experienced in the case of the Truthseeker, 180 tons, china stone; Four Brothers, 150 tons, pipeclay ; J.T.S., 230 tons, pipeclay ;John Clarke, 180 tons, china atone; Elizabeth Davy. 140 tons, china clay; Countess of Carrick, 165 tons, china clay; Guiding Star, 160 tons, chalk flints ; Romola, 150 tons, china clay, was given as an exatnple that mis.ttst be multiplied considerably. On Monday there were 30 vessels in dock idle, but it was admitted that a great improvement had taken place in the work, more vessels being in process of discharging than during the whole of the previous fortnight. An excuse had been put forward that the delay was caused through lack of warehouse room, but this the shipmas- ters denied; the delay, in their opinion, had arisen throug'e a want of proper system. The memorial askeol the council, in the interests of the shipmasters, in the interests of owners of craft, and in the interests of Run- corn itself, to take such action as would be best calcu- lated to remove the cause of complaint, and thus ensure a continuance of the present trade at the docks. The memorial was signed by 35 captains of vessels.—Captain Millar said that if this state ot atlairs was iaot altered the effect would be to drive the tradeto other ports such as Preston, Fleetwood. Ellestnere Port, and Barrew.— After considerable discussion Mr. Speakman said the council would do their utmost to cause the Ship Canal Company to improve the facilities for trade in Runcorn. Captain Millar also introduced another matter of great importance to the shipping community. He pointed out that ships having to remove from Weston Point Docks to Runcorn Docks in order to load at the latter place, hail to cross the Ship Canal, pass. the Weston Mersey Lock into the river, proceed up the river, then enter Bridgewater Lock, again cross the Ship Canal, and 30 enter the tidal basin of the company's own docks at Runcorn. The direct and convenient course for the ships was along the Ship Canal, but for traversing this short length of the canal, a charge of 2d. per ton en the registered tonnage was made, and no captain would incur that item at the present low rate of freight. The traffic through the two locks named was very heavysand the pas:age of "light " schooners under the circum- stances described was a needless interference with that traffic, and a disadvantage to all concerned. The ship- masters asked the council to use their influence with the company, to prevail upon the company to allow the shorter route to be used tress of toll.—Mr. Speakman said the council had had this matter in hand, and at a recent meeting in Mancheiter a deputation from the council was given to understand that this charge would be abol- ished.—Mr. Hewitt, a member of the council, put in a document showing that it was still made.—Mr. Speak- man promised that the necessary representations would be made to the company, and the deputation, having thanked the council, the interview terminated. CURIOUS ACCIDENT TO A S fEAMER ON THE

div.head: CANAL.
div.p: CANAL.

A con us aceident occurred to the steamer "Man- chester," trading between Belfa3t and Manchester, while coming up the canal near Runcorn on Tuesday. The captain noticed that all the " way " had gone off his ship which did not move though the engines worked. The vessel was afterwards towed to Manchester where on examination showed that the blades of the propeller had become loose and had dropped into the canal.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TIIESDAY.—Beforo his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. MANCHESTER Sun. CANAL V WILLIAM BURTON.—Tbe Manchester Ship Canal Company claimed from William Burton, flatowner, St. Georges Buildings Liverpool, £ll 7s. 7d. for damage done to coping stones of the Ship Canal wall at the Old Quay Lock, Runcorn. Mr. A. Newman, of Manchester, appeared on behalf of the Company, and Mr. T. Br.asley of Liverpool appeared for the defendant. Captain HarveV, lockmaster,stated that on March 31st about noon the steam fiat "Alice.' came up the Mersey, on the Lancashire side and observing that it was intended tc bring her into the lock, he twice shouted and made a signal for those in charge to pert the helm. His instructions were disregarded with the result that the craft collided with the wall and dis- placed five coping stones weighing several tons, and smashed two others.—This statement was corroborated by Captain Carr of the flat " Congreve, engineer to the company for the Runcorn section, stated that he considered the amount claimed a reasonable sum as they had had to replace one of the stones altogether. For the defence, the captain of the flat—William Hough- ton—stated that it was the first time they had been in the lock, and they were travelling all night to enter— George Houghton, mate, said they would have got in the locks all right if the sailing of the boat had not been taken out of their hands by CapZain Harvey. Their boat was old and rotten and the timber was in such a state that they could pull it away in handfulls. It was there- fore impossible for the " Alice "to do damage without injury to the boat and the vessel sustain-d no damage save that of having a quantity of tar scraped off the bluff of the bow. Toe Judge without hesitation said that the defence was hopeless, and gave judgment for the Canal Company, for the full amount claimed with costs.

SHIP CANAL.
THE 'TRAFFIC.

- -- The events of tbe past week are likely to have an im- portant effect upon the future of the Ship Canal. First, perhaps, in point of importance, is the visit of the general manager. Mr. Marshall Stevens, to the United States and Csuada, with the object of negotiating for the establishmrnt of regular lines of steamer J between north Atlantic ports and Manchester. Mr. Stevens cum- menced his journey eight days ago,and relying upon the correspondence received from representative people across the water, was sanguine of initiating great things in the course of his six weeks' tour. Another item of exceptional interest has been the arrival of the second consignment of Canadian cattle and sheep at the Alan- cheater Corporation's Foreien Animals' Wharf per the Furness liner Feliciana. The animals were landed in first-class condition, and were all bought up within a very few hours after being offered for sale. Following the arrival of the Feliciana came that of the Gulf of Genoa with the third shipment of freest) meat, rabbits, wool, and miscellaneous cargo from Australia in c )nnec- tion with the Greenock Steamship Company's service. A further matte r to which attention may be called is the tact that the Royal Prince has sailed for the Mediter- ranean with the largest cargo yet shipped from Man- chester to these ports. The owners of the line have made amp'' provision for dealing with the Egyptian cotton trade, the new season in connection with which opens next month, and are about to run larger and more suitabla vessels than was the case last season, in antici- pation of the heavy crop alteady foretold. The Ameri- can cotton trade will also Is cove.clue attention, Messrs. Watts, Watts, and Co. having intimated that they will resume sailioes from New Orleans and Galveston at fregnent intervals during the season, whilst the regular service of Messrs. Lamport and Bolt from New York will be continued. During the week ended Friday, 117 seagoing VeS4el3 passed alene the canal, 63 of this num- ber having entered and 54 passed outwards. Foreign traffic has accounted for 22 arrivals and 13 departeres, whilst 41 shins engaged in the coastwiso trade have en- tered and 41 left the canal.

WHOLESALE WINDOW-BREAKING AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday morning, a young militiaman named William Percy was charged with damaging windows in Brick-st.,Fennell-st. and other places at 2 &deck on Sunday morning.--He pleaded guilty.—Fanny Simpson, Fennell-et., stated that she had a window broken about midnight on Saturday night. —Martha Cook, licensee of the " Gardener's Arms," Brick-street, said that at 2 a.m. on Sunday she was in her kitchen when she heard a noise as of rowdy people coming down the street. Next she heard three panes of her front room window broken and then her sittingroten window. She looked out and saw three soldiers going up Battersby-lane and hitting at the windows. She reported the matter to the poliee.—P.C. Condliffa stated that at 2.15 on the day in questiAn he was on duty in Battersby-lane and met three soldiers going in the direction of Orford Barracks. They were laughing and shouting. On getting near the " Gardener's Arms' witness met Mrs. Cook who reported the window smash- ing to him. Witness went to the barracks and informed the Sergeant of the guard who brought two of the soldiers to him. Defendant was one of them, and be had the stick produced in his possession. Witness took him into custody and he admitted breaking ten windows in several different houses. Be appeared sober but looked as if he had had some drink during the night. Witness found that the other soldiers were not to blame in the matter.—Defendant stated that he was drunk and did not know what he was doing.—A Sergeant from the Barracks said that defendant had only been in the militia ten weeks and had already done a few days default. —The magistrates sent him to gaol for three months hard labour.

ALLEGED THEFT OF TALLOW.—John Mersey, of Nelson-st.. was brought up ol remand on a charge of stealing a barrel of tallow valued at V., the property of the United Alkali Com- pany on August 17. Mr Knowles, of Widnes, defended and prisoner pleaded guilty.—W•lliam Raiford said that he was the weighman at the United Alkali Company. He weighed and marked the tallow which lay in the dockside. He saw it last Saturday, there safe with others. There were only two belonging to this consignment. The man Massey lived in Nelson-street. near to the works, and had axorke I for the Company. In answer to Mr. Knowles. they had been troubled with children moving things and where the tallow was lying was only 20 yards from the gates. He never Saw the man near the tub o tallow.—Samuel Pope, manager at Hazlehurst Works ha, I seen the barrel of tallow wh'eh belonged to his Company. It was valued at 363. to 375. He ne7er saw the tallow in the works.but the barrel bad the mark of the man from whom they bought the tallow.—Cross examined, thee had suffered very considerable annoyance from children. lie might also say that they suf- fered from people sending children to pilfer fuel—John Cooper, box maker at Hazleherst works, said prisoner bor- rowed a truck from him on Tuesday morning, but lid not say what he wanted it for. He had to pass the tallow on the way back with the truck.—Nfr. Worrell wife cf William Worrall of I-toward-street. saw the man in Howard-street. last Monday in the forenoon. He had nothing with him, ut came for a truck and there was a barrel of tallow near the truck. He rolled the barrel to the wall, and left it there. She saw him again on Tuesday taking the ca3k away on a truck towards the Sprinch.—P.C. Gregory said that on Wed- nesday the 19th hist he found the barrel at the top end of Ellesmere-street and he afterwards went to the works and in consequence of informati. n he received, he apprehended the pilsoner. He charged him with stealing the ta,low and prisoner said he . knew nothing about it. For the arenas Mr. Knowles urged that there was not sufficient evidence to convict and pointed out that it was quite possible that the children who, it vies admitted. in- fested the works had rolled the tallow.—The magistrates gave the defendant the benefit of the d ,übt and dismissed the case. _ _ _

div.head: JAPAN AND ITS TRADE.
div.p: JAPAN AND ITS TRADE.

Some interesting facts are made public in a report just issued by ths Kireign Ofe dealing with the trade of Yokohama for the year 1895. The main feature of these returns lies in the steady increase indicated in Japan's toreign commerce. The total trade ef Yokonatna in 1895 was greater than in the previous by close upon £2.800,000. he exports in 1895 were £9.185.760, in 1894 £7.681,858; and the imports £5 893 042 and £5.410.501 recoectively : making totals of £15,081,832 and £13,092,359. The cliff Twice b-twe,-n the sums re- presents the substantial inerea,e of 15 ner cent. Com- paring the rate of increase in the case of the four coun- tries which are the leading participators in Japan's trade and taking imports and exports together, the statistics for Yokohama show that Germany is mak ng the most rapid advance and Great Britain the 10-west, the various rafts of increase in respect to the totals ef 1894 being : Germany. 53 per cont. : America, nearly 18 : French, 12i ; and Great Britain, less than 8. Taking the proportions in which the gross trade and the port is shared between the same countries, it is found that America heads the list with 34 per cent., Great Britain coming next with 21. France 17, and Germany 7. Of last year's total British trade, amount- ing to £4,675,000, two-thirds were to the United King- dom itself, one-sixth to Hong Kong, and the remaining one-sixth was distributed between India, Canada, and Australia. The Australian trade amounted in all to only £lOO,OOO, hut it is significant that this sum was double that of the year before, and that the hulk of it consisted of imports, mostly wool. In regard to imports generally, two classes of manufacture show a marked increase, woolen fabrics and metallic geods—a difference which the report attributes to the war. Cloths of onixed material including shoddy wefts, betrayed a falling off et 60 per cent., and, it is stated, are certain to dwindle out of consumption. The improvement in nearly all branches of metal is most marked, exhibiting. if wire nails be left out of account, an increase of ever 34 per cent, in quantity and value. It is, however, to be noted that most of the bar and plate iron is now of Continental makes, the import from England being apparently on the decline.
