SINGULAR CHILD STEALING CHARGE AT CREWE.

At Crewe, on Tuesday, last week the magistrates wer occupied several hours in hearing a charge of stealing e child, preferred against a young married couple named Thomas and Nellie Green, of Ashton-under-Lyne. Rhoda Hodges, a single woman, said that on Friday last she was at a lodging-house in Oak-street, Crewe, with her four children. That night they were all in one bed. The two prisoners occupied a bed in the same room. Being somewhat crowded with her children, she complained, and the prisoners asked her to hand over to them the baby, aged five months. She did so and went back to bed. On getting up she missed both the prisoners and the baby. She was told they had left the house at five o'clock. She went to the railway station, but could not trace them. She obtained a war- rant for their apprehension. In reply to the prisoners, the prosecutrix denied that she ill•treated the baby and had offered it to several persons. P.C. Richardson said he apprehended the prisoners near Wheelock Hcath.They both said the mother gave them the child The female prisoner said the mother told her she could have the child, and she took it. ut of pity. Margaret Lee said she was in the bedroom of the lodging-house, and heard the conversation. Nellie Green said, "if you are tired of the baby, give it to me," and the prosecu- trix got out of bed,took the baby to the female prisoner, and said she could keep it. The next morning, the two prisoners got up and took the child downstairs. The mother had told them the night before where to find the child's clean clothes. Before the baby was taken away a Mrs. Hulse came upstairs and told the mother that the prisoners were going to take the child with them, and the mother said, " Let them take it." Sarah Ankers, another witness, said she heard the mother say she wished she could get rid of her children. She saw her give the baby to the prisoners, and she heard her say she could keep it. John Malone said the prosecutrix had given the child away twice since she had been stay- ing at the lodging-house. The prosecutrix had also given another of her children to an organ grinder, but he returned it after keeping it a week. The bench thought no jury would convict the prisoners of stealing the child, and discharged them.

RECENT BABYLONIAN DISCOVERIES. The Constantinople correspondent of the "Dsily News" writes :—The discoveries made by two expeditions that have been and are still working in Babylonia are certain to arouse general interest. A French expedition has for some time been at work at Telo, and has been remark- ably successful. But the American expedition has pro- duced even more remarkable results. The finnan au- tbgrising the Americans to explore the mound of Nippur or, Niffur, was granted eight years ago. It was at Nippur that Sir Henry (then Mr.) Layard nearly lost his life from the attacks of the Arabs. The University of Penn- sylvania undertook an expedition at its own expense, and the Rev. Dr. Peters, an Episcopal clergyman, now in Charge of a church in New York, was placed at the head of exploring party intended t excavate at Nip- pur. He was aided by Mr. Haines,a young Mill who had been a tutor in Robert College, and who still continues connected with the explorations. At presen the head of the expedition is Professor Hilprecht, an American who occupies a foremost place in everything relating to Baby- lonian arclueology. Upon him has devolved the task of classifying and deciphering the enormous number of inscriptions which have been found at Nippur. The labour of piecing together the thousands of fragments of vases and other objects, and of deciphering the in- scriptions upon them,has during the past winter nearly cost him his eyesight. Happily he is now recovering, and is at present in Constantinople arranging and c.ilassi- fying the inscriptions and ()fleets of priceless value, which under the conditions of the firman become the property of the imperial Museum. Professor Elilprecht informed me that it will be years before the Pennsylvania University will be able to pub- lish all the inscriptions which have been deciphered, but the publication has already begun, and gives promise of a rich harvest. The first and most notable result of the excavations is that the history of the Babylonian people as recorded in cuneiform writing on tablets is carried back at least 2,250 years further than it had yet been known. In other words, there is ' now abundant written evidence that the Babylonian people existed, and were civilised enough to be able to write, at least seven thousand years before Christ. In conversation st ith the Professor, who in all matters of erase logy is cautious, I asked whether he could say that the written records did not go further back. He replied that in his judgment they probably went back as far as eight thousand years n C., but that in his published reco,ds he was unwilling to print anything which could not be amply borne out by evidence. To have pushed bas:k written history at one stroke by 2,250 years is, however, enough to make a reputation. In reply to my inquiry how it happened that his predecessor had not found the many objects belonging to this early period, lie explained that Dr. Peters, to whom he attri- buted great credit for the manner in which he had opened out the great mound at Nipper, had worked down to a certain floor or platform which he and others had taken to be the grcund level of that ancient city. One of the party, however.suggested that this level should he pene- trated and digging centinued until rock or virgin soil was reached. This suggestion was adopted, and to the delight of all concerned it was found that what had been taken for the level of the ancient city was only the level of a comparatively modern city built over the ruins of an older one or a succession of older ones. The excava- tions above the level or platform had gone through 36ft. of debris': They were now continued to a depth f 301 t. below it. The excavations above the platform discovered remains which covered a period of 4,000 years of Baby- lonian histcry. Below the platform to the virgin soil was an accumulation of drains, preserved and broken pottery, and various other objects of interest. Twenty- three feet below the platform Mr. Haines came upon the most ancient keystone arch known, an arch which Professor Hdprecht thinks cannot be later than 5,000 B.C. Last summer, Mr. Haines, who has spent the last three years in continous work at Nippur, excavated the lower part of the marvellous wall of the city. Its foundatiens were found to be sixteen feet below the level of the desert ; the wall itself was seventeen feet high and forty-five feet wide. Upon the sop of this wall was another of unknown height. These walls were built of bricks twenty inches square—prob- ably the largest bricks ever used. The most valuable finds, however, were the inscriptions upon broken vases, bricks, tablets,and many other objects, and from these it is confidently predicted by Professor flilprecht that a continuous history f Babylonism will be able to be o written. Among the recent finds of the French expedition which has been, and is still, working at Telo, are a num- ber of dated cuneiform tablets of Sargon the First and his son Naram-Sin. These have now reached Constan- tinoPle, and within the last two months have been sub- mitted to the examination of Monsieur fiensay, director of the Museum of the L' uvre, and of Professor Hil- Precht, who has been retained by the Turkish Govern- ment to decipker and classify the objects found by both expeditions. By this important fini all questions as to the mythical character of Sargon is put an end to. and he is shown to have been a real pers-n. 'nib con- tents of the so-called Oman tablet are definitely decided to be historical and not mythical. One of the new tab- lets speaks of "the year when Sargon marched against Palestine" (Martu). This was 3,800 BC. Even were no ether finds to be made the inscriptions gathered by the two expeditions will add largely to the knowledge possessed of the history and civilisation of Babylonia. .s. .

The truth is, however, that there is every reason to sup- pos” that there exists an untold store of archeological riches buried along the shores of the Euphrates and Tieris. Books on the subject which were up to date three years agn already require revision, and there is reason to believe that the efforts which the Americans and the French are making in a field first opered by Layard will be amply rewarded.

CUPID.

olish Cupid, full of life, Heeding not this world of strife; Be is blind but merry too— ithout him what should we do? Silly Cupid loves to greet Ages that uneven meet. Rich and poor he cannot see, All alike to him must be. We are often lead astray, Far from wisdom's better way, Far from sunny fields of joy, Weeping for the darling boy. Though we sigh to think him blind, Surely we shall never find One so charming who can see Vice's faults and misery. Pride and cupid ne'er agree; Pride is tull of enmity, Cupid should be free and gay, With cold pride he cannot stay. Where the crystal fount; ins spring Youths with happy maidens sing ; Cupid dear will ever be Glad amid life's mystery.
Warrington.
S. KENYON.

div.head: VILLAGE BANKS.
div.p: VILLAGE BANKS.

The establishment of agricultural banks or village credit societies, although not proceeding as rapidly as might be expected, is making steady progress ; and in places where they have been started the results so far have proved satisfactory. Since the beginning of the year five societies have come into existence, making a total of eight in the rural districts in England. A society is formed in a village on co-operative principles, with the object of providing small occupiers, allotment hol- ders, village tradesmen, and the like with timely assist- ance in the shape of a little capital at a low rate of interest, the sums borrowed being applied to specific purposes approved by the committee. Some idea of the extent of the operations of the eight societies which have been started may be gathered from the following figures :—The aggregate capital amounts in round numbers to £691, subscribed by one hundred and fifty members, thirty loans having been granted. in the smaller societies the loans are limited to from £5 to £lo,but the larger banks extend the noaxi• mum to as much as £5O. In every case the banks aro said to be proving most useful,and the Lumber of mem- bers tends to increase as the benefits become more widely understood. A society is not started as a profit making concern ,and the rate of interest paid to deposi- tors is fixed (say) at 3 per cent., while the interest charged to borrowers is ri3t more than six per cent. the margin at 3 per cent. covering working expenses and then ucleus of reserve fund.

div.head: KAISER'S TABLE.
div.p: THE KAISER'S TABLE.

Thanks to the researches of Oscar Kaufmann the whole world can now learn without difficulty not only "upon what meat doth this our Kaiser feed," but the exact conditions that regulate the diet of the Im- perial Family of Germany. Housekeeping, as we understand it, forms no part of William cares, as he coottacts for his meals on a fixed scale of payment. The dinner ordinarily served costs 7a. 61. per head,but this modest tariff is raised to £1 or 303. on grand occasions. Each morning a menu is submitted to the Empress,but when a State banquet is given the Grand Marshal of the Court supervises the bill of fare. Three meals a day suffize as a rule t-) satisty the crav- ings of the Imperial appetite. Breakfast,at nine o'clock or earlier, is quite a British repast, consisting of tea, coffee,eggs, beefsteaks, and mutton or veal cutlets. At two comes a simple lunch of soup, roast meats and vege- tables, and a single sweet dish. The dinner hour, save under extraordinary circumstances, is not later than six ani seldom lasts an hour. Six courses are served, and the party nearly always amounts to sixty persons. Bor- deaux, Rhine wine, Moselle, and champagne always ap- pear on the Imperial table, with now and then a bottle of Tokay or some costly vintage, but the Emperor him- self drinks very little,
DAMAGE TO PROPERTY BY SMALL BOYS. POLICE PROCEEDINGS.

()n Friday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court,before Alderman Harrison and Councillor Roberts, two cases were heard in which boys of tender age were summoned for committing damage to property. The first involved Arthur Gilbert, aged 10, of 10, School- street, and Thomas Grounds, aged 12, of Kent-street. They were charged with having on the 13th July dam- aged a sleeper fence, the property of the L. and N.-W. Railway Company, by setting fire to it.—Mr. gland, solicitor, prosecuted and said he was almost ashamed to bring such small boys before the Court, but it was necessary as a warning to boys given to m's ch!evous pranks. On the day in question one of the Company's servants was passing down the line between Arpley and Latchford when he noticed the sleeper fence on the up-side, blazing, He put the fire out but neat morning the fence:was burning again.—James William James,relief porter,corroborated as to the fence burning.—Detective Parsons said he had made enquiries and Lund the defendants who admitted that they had set the fence on fire.—A still smaller boy, not charged, was called, and he stated which part the defendant's took in the action. —Alderman Harrison : What part did you do. The boy (innocently): I struck the match. (Laughter).—Mr. Stansfield. master of St. James school. where the boys attended, gave them a good character. He thought they had no intention of doing damage but having matches, etc., they were anxious to makes fire. He always tried to influence the boys outside the school and to some extent succeeded.— Councillor Roberts: I think your schocl is very well managed. I see a good deal of it and a goo 1 deal of your boys, and I think it reflects great credit upon you.—Mr. Stansfield : Thank you.—The Chairman pointed out the wrong the boys had done, and said they would im- pose a penalty of the costs only. Four boys from the neighbourhoed of Warburton-st. and all about 7 years of age, namely, Thomas Griffin, Thomas Moran, John Moran, and Thomas Hudson, were charged with committing damage to planks and barrows the property of Mr. James Grace —Mr Grace said th it for the last six months his premises had been made a plat gr,-.und of by children. They burrowed under the fencing and threw stones on to the roof, breaking a large number of slates. He was hound to bring these procecdings to protect his property. The taking out of the summons had had a very salutary effect, and he did not wish to press the case against these boys whom he had caught on the premises.—The parents of the youth ful delinquents said it was older boys who did the dam- age.—The Chairman was about to order the two Morans who had turned 7, to pay costs. when Mr. Grace offered to withdraw the case if the parents would promise to keep their children away.—The mothers gave the re- quired promise, and the boys were dismissed.

div.head: DEATH FROM DIPHTHERIA IN AN
div.p: DEATH FROM DIPHTHERIA IN AN
OMNIBUS.
EXTRAORDINARY CASE.

On Thursday, last week, Mr.Schroderlheld an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Daisy Clieriton,aged two years,the daughter of a labourer,who died while in an omnibus on Westminster Bridge.la °pet - ing the iequiry the Coroner said he understood that tie child was taken to Westminster Hospital in a dying con- dition, but the house surgeon would not admit it, but told the mother to take it home, and he (the Coroner) was informed that the doctor reported the child to be suffering from diphtheria. The child was taken away, but died in the 'bus on the way home.— Emily Cheriton the mother, s:ated that the child had lately been left in charge of her mother. The child became very ill, and she took it on Monday morning to the Westminster Hospital. The doctor asked if the child had had diphtheria,and witness said no, but asked him to take the child in. He said he could not do so. as all the beds were full. So she asked for some medicine, which he also refused He did not say what was the cause of the child's illness, but told her to take it home at once and call in the parish do - tor. Witness took the child away, first to her mother, and then got into an omnibus to go home. Just as the 'bus got over the bridge, the child seemed dying, so she got out and went to St. Thomas's Hospital, but the doctor there said the child was dead. Witness had had no idea the child was suffering from diphtheria when she got into the omnibus.—William Cheriton, the bus• band, stated that he was only earning Gs. a week. (Sen- sation). Out of this he allowed his in it her-in-law 33. a week forthe child's keep, and tried to keep his wife and 'himself on the rest.—Dr. Genge, house-Angeon at West- minster Hospital, deposed that he saw the child and found it had diphtheria very badly. The disease had spread into the lungs, whilst it was already too late to psrform tracheotomy. Witness saw the child was likely to dieat any moment, but as all the beds were full ho advised the mother to take the child home. Wit. nese did not think the mother would take it into a public vehicle, although he did not tell her not to do so.—The Coroner : Do yeti think it was dangerous her taking it into a 'has ?—Witness : Yes, undoubtedly.— The Coroner : Could not you have placed the child in the casual ward and have sent for the fever hosptta.l ant horities ?—Witness : We could not take such a cam- plaint into the casual ward. It would not be safe.—The Secret ary oh the Westminster Hospital stated that all the infectious diseases wards at the hospital were full, but the house surgeon could have sent the child to the isolated room while the ambulance was sent for, but at present the asylum's attendants were very busy, and possibly a six hours' delay would have been caussd.— The Coroner said he.stiould have thought it would have been for better to aave done that than send the case away into the public streets andess the case proved, into a public conveyance.—Ultimately the jury returned a verdict of death from natural causes.

ROMANCE OF A HANGMAN.
AN EXTRAORDINARY HISTORY

Mysterious disappearance seems to be the inevitable fate of nearly every hangman, the latest to fade silently away being the official hangman. of Victoria, says the 'Sydney Uulletin." The man's history is a remarkable one. he was the son of a wealthy English manufac- turer, and received an excellent education. In 1880 he reached Melbourne under engagement to a big wine and spirit firm as head traveller at a salary of £5OO per year, nut after a couple of years of the work he decided to strike out "on his own," and bought a suburban hotel. This he kept with fair success until 1885, when he sold out and returned to England. There he received a sum of £5,000 from his father for the purpose of starting in business, but an 18 months' jaunt over Europe and the States was more to his liking, and when he arrived in Melbourne he had scarcely a penny to bless himself with. Half-a-dozen templrary warders being required at Pent- ridge Prison,he put in an application and was appointed and it was while in that capacity that he became acquainted with Jones, the nangman, who suicided rather than hang Mrs. Knorr. There seemed to be some magnetic sympathy between the men from the first, for they " pard up " immediately and off duty were seldom seen apart. The budding hangman soon got transferred to the police force. In 1888 he left the force 'for more lucrative employment," say the records; but this employment, whatever it was, doesn't seem to have lasted long, for in a few months he is found taking his first lesson in hangmatiship at Bal beret Gaol, when he acted as Jones's assistant. He heat migrated to Sydney, where he earned an honest livin doing a "bit of flogging at the various gaols. But the work was laborious; he was .imbitious. So when Jones cut his throat two days before the date of Mrs. Knorr's hanging, his churn deferred weeping over his old friend until he had penned and posted an application for the vacant billet. This letter was successful, and, starting by the next train south, he arrived in Melbourne in good time, and the job which oven Jones, the slayer of 20 men, had shrunk from committing, was taken on by his deli- cately nurtured and highly educated friend. A little romance forms a pretty sequel to the story. Within a month after the demise of the esteemed Jones, the new hangman led to the altar a blushing bride—the widow ef his predecessor.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND HIS CONSERVATIVE CRITICS.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND HIS CONSERVATIVE CRITICS.

Mr. J. M. Maclean,the Conservative member for Car- diff, recently addressed a letter to the "Western Mail,' in which be criticised Mr. Chamberlain's manageinent of South African affairs,especially in the Transvaal. A. correspondent who forwarded a copy of Mr. Maclean's letter to Mr. Chamberlain has received the following re- ply :—" Highbury, Moor Green, Birmingham, August 20th, 1896. Sir,-1 am directed by Mr. Chamberlain to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 18th inst. calling attention to a letter from Mr. J. M. Maclean in the Western Mail,' and to say in reply that neither the tone nor the substance of the same justifies him in tak- ing any notice of it.—l am, sir, yours faithfully, Joitit Wirsos."—On Monday evening Mr. Maclean issued the following rejoinder :—" It grieves me to the heart to have incurred the serious displeasure of Mr. Chamber- lain. The' tone 'of his own criticisms of public mem has always been so meek, and their 'substance 'so ac- curate, that his high resolve not to take notice of my rough and careless statements seem quite natural. I ant to some extent,however,consoled for his dignified rebuke by the widespread publicity which my letter of the Western Mail' has obtained,and by the numerous corn munications I have received from correspondents in various parts of the country, who thank rae warmly for lhaving expressed their views.

THE TOWN CLERK.

Sir,—ln your issue of the) 15th inst. Pppeared an announcensent that we are in danger of tubing the ser- vices of our respected Town Clerk. If such is to be the case I fea it would he n loos to the town. There can be no question that Mr. Whittle we hate a thc roughly capable, and tiii cot officer. He is certainly devoted to his work and has the welfare and advancement of the tuwn well at heart. As a large ratepayer I (and I am sore the ratepayers generally) should be glad if our representatives would take steps with the object oc getting Mr. Whittle to re- main with us. The improvements in the town since he was appointed six years age have been numerouo and important and there still remains a great deal to be done. Now that we have the right man in the right place, why not keep him? I enclose my card.—Yours, ttc., C. W.

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

" Oom Paul" has his private troubles. His wife's hcalth is a source of anxiety to him, and recently his married sister, whose maiden name was Sophia Mar- gareta Kruger,died at Steenbok fontein,Rustenberg. Mrs.. Pieter du Plessis had attained the age of seventy-seven years. and was highly respected in the Rustenberg dis- trict of the Transvaal. She was the President's favour- ite sister, was married at seventeen, and leaves behind her a total of 170 children, grandchildren, and great grandchildren. One of her sons, "Om Casper," is a member of the Second Raad. However stern he may be,when occasion requires. President Kruger has strong family affections,and he was deeply affected by the lois of a sister which left him the last of a family of six. The President himself has 142 descendants.

There are some curiosities in the dietary customs of the people. Coeoa and chocolate are going up in popu- lar estimation and demand,. whereas coffee is falling,the revenue for the past financial year having dropped two per cent. Tea has gone up nine million pounds in con- sumption—an increase of more than four per cent. to the revenue. Rum declines, but the brandy consumed, say the Commisioners, by the wealthier classes rises and falls so as to indicate the spending power ot those classes. It went up last year. AU kinds of wines, which have been uniformly redueing in the yield to the revenue for the last twenty years have alsc gone up, and the in- crease in tobacco amounts to one-third of a million.

The Postmaster-General reports that from a financial ' point of view the past year was one of unexampled prosperity in the Post Office. The general election and the revival in trade combined to enable the Department to produce a profit of £3,632,122. The number of letters dealt with was 1,834,000,000,and there were 78,839,610 telegrams of all descriptions. The total number of pos- tal packets was 3,030.000,000, as against an average of 2,817.000,000 in the five preceding years. The parcels delivered in the United Kingdom showed an increase of 5.9 per cent., and those sent to or received from places abroad an increase of 13 per cent. The inland money- order business maintained its tendency to increase, and the Post-office Savings Bank business also ivareased con- siderably.

Tha German custom of duelling has borne singular fruit at Konigsberg. The manager of the liorsengarten, a concert garden there,ref used the challenge of a Govern- ment assessor. The higher Government officials of the city have therefore,according to a" Standard "telegram boycotted the establishment,and the General Command- ing has forbidden officers to frequent it, and hag with- drawn the permission granted to the regimental bands to play there.

Prince Max of Saxony officiated as deacon during the High Mass at the German Church, Whitechapel,on Sun- day. He also preached an eloquent sermon in GermAn on the Gospel of the day. In the afternoon he held a reception of the leading members of the German colony in London. At the evening servine during Benediction be officiated as deacon. An enthusiastic reception was accorded him on entering the Ge-ellver2in, the hall being crowded with Germans from all parts of London, in- ciuding Count Walderleben. Baron Von Limburg, the Very Rev. Dr. Triebs, and Father Weber. The Rev. Father Sanders introduced the Prince in a felicitous speech, after which the whole companv rose and cheered heartily with the usual German" Hoch ! boch ! hoch !" The prince made a suitable reply, saying that they must Rot look upon him as a Prince. but simply as a priest, which really was a more noble title. He said that he had come to labour amongst working men, and in this respect our Lord set the example, for He Himself was a working man, who laboured for the good of others, and particularly the poor. The greatest goodwill prevailed amongst the audience, and everything passed off satis - factorily. His Royal Highness speaks English fluently. He has renounced his rights to the Saxon throne on be- coming a priest—his father being heir to the throne.

In addition to a scheme for the formation of a fund for the insurance of all municipal property aqainst losses by fire, the Corporation of Glasgow have under consider- ation a proposal which would, it is claimed, prove a boon to the humbler classes of -citizens. Either through negligence or other cause, few of the smaller househol- ders insure their property, and the consequence is that when a fire occurs in their dwellings they have no com- pensation for a loss which they are little able to bear. The proposal is that the Corporation should undertake this duty for all tenants whose rents are under £lO per annum, taking them to an extent not exceeding 41. per £l. That is to say, a tenant paying a rental of £4 per annum would be taxed to the extent of not more than 4d., while one with a rental of £8 19s. would pay a tax of 10d. There would be corresponding rates of compen satios, the maximum being probably £5O, while the £4 tenant would not get more than £2O, the details of the loss being proved by the tenant, as under an ordinary insurance policy.

The poor woman who a few days ago found £1.25 in bank notes in Hanover Square, and was not rewarded at all, again appeared at the Marlborough•street Police Court, London, en Monday. On seeing her the mar.is- , trate (Mr. Hannay) said: You must remain a little whilo. I have something for you that will gladden your heart. After the other applications had been heard Mr. Hannay told the woman that it was very fortunate that her name and address had been taken. It was impos- sible to take the names of all applicants, but in her case it had been done or she cculd not have been emmoni• cated with. Several people had sympathised with her, and had between them sent the sum of for her. He had thought first of putting the money in the Post-office Saving's Bank for her, so that she might take greater care of it.—The applicant said she did not spend her money wastefully. She was a tailoress, and would en- deavour to start in business with the money, but could not in her present condition make a start.—Mr. Hannay gave her 22a. to go on with, and told her to call again on Wednesday.

Mr. Colenbrander, who was specially sent for by the tdatabele chiefs in order to discuss the terms of sur- render, has led a highly adventurous life. He is an Afrikander, and was for many years in Zululand, where be took part in tribal fights. In one of these he received a fearful blow from a battle-axe, and was left for dead, but revived and crawled to a place of safety. He mar- ried a Durban lady. who is a keen sportswoman and interested in :Ale pursuit of big game. He was one of the original settlers in Mashonalatd, and took Dart in the fighting which resulted in the overthrow of Loben." gula. Mr. Colenbrander is said to be as much feared as be is trusted by the Matabele.

The American papers continue to print appalling lists o'f•the victime of what is tersely known as the "heat plague." In New York the suffocating temperature has driven thousands of people to piers on the East and North Itivers, and beds have been made up on the roofs w,herewer possible. Over in Br)oklyn, according to the "New York World," the park afficials have suspended their regulations, an that thousands of men and women, in whose apartments the temperature approaches that of a Turkish bath, have been allowed to take quilts and pillows into tl-e park and stretch themselves under the trees for .a cool sleep. One day recently there wae a record of more than a dozen persons at New York who fell from roofs and fire-escapes, whence they had gone to gather whatever breeze was blowing and to secure a night's sleep. Some of these folk were killed, and the rest were seriously injured. Many who went to sleep on the piers fell into the water and were rescued with diffl- cultr. Three or four of them were drowned. All the public baths were kept open night and day.

div.p: ODDYELLOWSHIP AT COLLIN'S GREEN.

On Laturday afternoon the Farmers' Refuge Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, MAJ. whose headquarters are at the Pear Tree Hotel, Collins Green, held their annual festival. A pro- cession was formed at the Pear Tree at 2 o'clock, about 60 taking part, and headed by the Earles- town brass band, paraded the district by way of the Brewery, Burtonweod Cottages, the Church and the Vicarage returning to the Pear Tree Hotel about .5-15. An excellent dinner was afterwards served by Mr. R. Naylor, 66 members and friends partaking thereof. Among the visitors was Bro. Dutton, C.S. St. Helens district. After dinner the table was cleared, and the proceedings were presided over by Bro. Dutton, the vice chair being occupied by Bro. Vose.—The usual loyal toasts were proposed and duly honoured. ."Prosperity to the Farmer Refuge Lodge " was responded to by Bro. W. Sephton, secretary, who in the course of his remarks said the lodge started the year with .£1.20, and had since deposited .C4O and had so-nething like. another £4O in hand. Altogether they were making good pro- gress, they had made. 9 new members this year and 4 others were proposed, the lodge 'being in a satis- factory position. During the evening emblems neatly framed in oak, were presented by Bro. Dut- ton, on behalf of the lodge to Bros. Sephton,P.G., secretary. M. Brown. P.G. and C. Massey, P.G.—The proceedings were enjoyably enlivened by songs, &c., contributed by Bros. James Doran, T. Traverse, J. Unsworth aad others. GOOD TEMPLAR DISTRICT LODGE SRatioN AT

div.head: E.A.RLESTOWN.
div.p: E.A.RLESTOWN.

rho quarterly session of the district lodge of South-west Lancashire was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Saturday. The session was opened at 2.30 under the presidency ot Bro. J. A. Lee D.C.T., of Liverpool, nearly every officer in the district being present. There was also a large at- tendance of representatives and delegates from lodges in all parts of the district, together with the following visitors, Bros. Q.M.-Sergt. L. R. Driffield D.C.T., of Malta, J. B. Davies P.G.G., of Manchester, and sister Collings, of Birmingham. The report of the D.C.T. Bro. Leo was received, in which a recom- mendation was made for holding a universal bazaar in aid of the Order. The question of a mileage fund for representaives attending the district lodge meetings was introduced and allowed to stand over for further consideratien. The report of the D. Sec. showed that there were 48 lodges in the district with 2.368 membeis. Bro. R. D. Patterson, D. Treas. showed the finances to be in a healthy con- dition with a balance of over .£9. The report of Bro. G. Clarke D.E.S. showed that open-air miesions had been general throughout the district at which the necessity for the complete suppression of the liquor traffic received prompt attention. He should have been pleased to have reported action by various lodges in opposition to the granting of licenses at Brewster Sessions. He had no doubt a number of such cases might be men- tioned, but the only places he was able to speak confidently about were Bedford Leigh and Ashton. With regard to Leigh he had been casually informed by a representative that opposition to the issue of licenses was to be offered, and to Ashton he could refer more definitely. On the outskirts of the town between Brynn'and Stubshaw Cross there was quite a large colony of comparatively new working ' class dwellings, and on a very eligible corner plot, the present holder of an outdoor license was anxiousl to have erected a large public-house. Already three applications had been made and refused, and a very strenuous effort was being made with the view of getting a license for premiees about to be erected, and amongst others the members of the Ashton Excelsior Lodge were determined to oppose the application. Not a single application for a new license ought to go unchallenged, and in many cases transfer of licenses too could be successfully opposed. In the discussion which followed, Bro. Ridings, of Ormskirk said that no G.T. lodge could as a body present a memorial against licenses to the Bench ; they must have a solicitor to represent them. Property owners, he said, were taking action, so that there was no necessity for the lodges to do anything. Bro. Boreland, D.S. Alliance, Liverpool, said there was a larger number of lic- enses being applied for than usual, but there was general activity in Liverpool against old and new licenses. Be said copies of resolutions passed at public meetings of ratepayers could be sent to the Magistrate's Clerk, who would read them to the Bench, but the latter would not receive such resolu- tions direct. The report was adopted. Earnest addresses were given by Bros. Driffiekl and Davies, and 22 candidates were initiated. The session was then closed and a public tea was held, at which about 120 persons were present. A public meeting followed, over which Bro. E. .T. George pre-ided there bring a very large attendance. Addresses were given by the Chairmen, Bros. R. W. Kirk us, P.D.C.T,, Liverpool, and Rev. .1. A. Lee. -ong-, recitations, &c., were given by Bro.. Snr,-.. Clarke, W. Wilson, Bowler, Forster, Sisters Jaktkson, and Ord.

div.head: EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL SEASON,
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL SEASON,

The prospects of the Eiriestown Association club during the coming sea-on are very favourable, notwithstanding that they have lost two or three of their best players. It will b remembered that they won the Lancashire Alhalite Championship, and this year they have entered besides the Alli- ance for the Lancashire Junior Cap and the Wigan and District Cup. They will start the present sea- son under promising contlitions, being free from debt, and given a good team with plenty of support from the public, they may reasonably ex- pect a successful season. They have lost three good players, viz., Arthur Lee (outside left.), Jos. Lee (goalkeeper), both of whom hive signed for Stockport County, and Charles (' Cap') Lee (inside right), who has joined Haydock, but his brother James, centre forward, has so tar not yet signed for anyone. With these exceptions ttie teams will re- main much the same as last year, but several new additions have been made. First and foremost, the club have secured Edwards, late of Horwich, as goalkeeper, and he Comes with a good reputation. In addition to last season's half hacks, Jones (War- rington St. Elphiti's), Roe ( Barn ton), Forbe3 (War- rington), Ramsey (Golborne). have been signed, so that it will be seen the committee will be in posFossion of plenty of ch ice. Clib- born has also signed as half back, but owing to an injury received in running, it is not expected he will be able to play before Christ- mas. For forwards the committee will depend upon Edmondson, Hughes, Maitland (late of Ain- tree Church) Harrison, Hall, (late o f Golborne) Mottram and Daniels (Liverpool). For the first time for several years, the club will this season run a reserve team, which they have entered in the West Lancashire and District League. Most of the members of the Victoria club, which has been dis- solved, and being a fairly good lot can be relied .upon to till vacancies which might arise in the first eleven. A fall list of fixtures has been arranged for the reserve, and. they may be expected to give a good account of themselves. Notwithstanding the inclemency of the weather, there was again a good muster at the P.S.A. meeting on Sunday. The proceedings were opened with singing, the scripture lesson was read by Mr. Bick- ford, and Mr. Clegg, secretary, presided. Mr. ttickman gave an excellent address, his subject being "Christ and the woman of Samaria." Mr. Mills contributed two solos, and Mr. Richardson was heard to good effect upon the cornet. The hearty singing of the hymn "Forward, brothers, forward," brought the meeting to a close. WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. The monthly meeting was held at Market-gate Chambers on Monday, Mr. F. Monks, J.P., in the chair. The Chairman and Messrs. John Fairclough and John Houghton were appointed as the dele- gates of the Chamber to the autumnal meeting of the Associated Chambers, to be held at Southamp- ton about the middle of next month. The Secretary (Councillor Arthur Bennett) has made arrangements with Mr. itadeley by which various Blue Books, Consular Reports, and particulars of International Tariffs, together with a large assortment of miscel- laneous commercial literature, after being filed at the offices of the Chamber for the convenience of the members, will be periodically forwarded to the Library for the use of the general public and kept Ifor permanent reference. VOLUNTEER INTELLIGENCR. There was a battalion drill on Saturday. Nine officers, sixteen sergeants and 101 others of the Warrington Volunteers fell in at the Drill Hall at 3 p.m. and marched to the recreation ground in Bank Park. Several interesting battalion move- ments were gone through by the men, under the direction of Majoe Widdows, after which they were marched back to the Drill Hall, where tea was pro- vided prior to being dismissed. Lieutenant-Colonel J. C. Ridgway was in command.—Class firing will take place on the 27th inst. at Altcar, and second and first class firing for" A" Company on the 29th inst., and the same for" F Company on the sth September. At the fortnightly meeting of Otidlellows Bene- volent Star Lodge No. 449, Warrington District, held at Mr. Belshaw'e, Horsematket-st., a presenta- tion was made to Bro. Allcock for past service ren- dered to the lodge. The presentation took the form of at emblem of the Order. Bro. Entwistle made the presentation. and in a brief speech thanked Bro. Allcock for his services and said that he had known him for a considerable time. He had always dis- charged the duties entrusted to him in a most satis- factory manner, and he hoped that Bro. CUTLERY and Electro-Plated GOODS.—GARLAND, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. A. LANG, JUN. On Tuesday, the grave closed over the remains of Arthur Lang, jun., younger son of Mr. Lang, who represents St. John's ward on the Board of Guar- dians. The deceased was in his seventeenth year and previous to his death he worked in the labora- tory at Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, Limited. On Saturday, he suc,ciambsd to an attack of enteric fever. Prior to proceeding to the Cemetery, a short service was conducted by the Rev. J. Tonge at the residence of Mr. Lang, in Parker-street. Amongst those present at the funeral were Mr. Lang (father), Mr. J. Lang (brother), Messrs. Hawthorn, Studer, Rose, Ruddock, Marshall, Ashton, Walker, Robin- son, G. Brown, D. Owen, Bristow, R. Travis, R. Atkinson, and a number of members of the class with which the deceased was connected at Wycliffe Sunday school. The coffin was reverentially borne to its last resting place by a number of the deceassd's fellow-workers at the laboratory. A large number of floral tributes had been sent by friends, including one from the members of the Sunday school class. IRON and BRAS BRDSTI4ADS--GARLAND, Iron- ranger. Warrington.—Advt. MORE BURGLARIES—SANKEY BRIDGES VISITED. The district does not seem to be free from bur- glars even yet as there have been some suspicious occurrences at Sankey Bridges. Late on Sunday seseina a man was noticed suspiciously prowling behind premises in Farrell-street, and on being questioned he said he was "looking for a night's lodgings." At midnight on Sunday some persons were heard running down the passage at the rear of the premises in Dale-street, and exclaiming in a loud voice " We've left the door open." A small shop in lioward-street has been broken into, and 2s. worth of goods taken from the premises. The house of J. Oliver, who resides at 31, Wright-street, Sankey Bridges, was visited on Sunday at midnight. Oliver is a furnaceman employed at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works, and when preparing to go out of the house in the early morning he heard a loud tapping at the kitchen window. His wife,who was not aware of what was going on, began to call a lo iger named Ennis Doherty. his disturbed the thieves, and they quickly decamped. The putty of the window had been chiselled out, leaving traces that the burglars had formed a determination to force the catch.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Monday evening. Bro. W. Wilson pre- sided, and there was a large attendance of members and visitors. One candidate was admitted to mem- bership.—The report of the District Lodge session was given by Bro. G. Clarke and adopted. A very earnest address was given by Bro. James Woods, and a programme of songs and readings by various members of the lodge brought an enjoyable evening to a close. WARGRAVE CHURCH BAZAAR. As will be seen by an advertisement in another olumn, a three days' bazaar in aid of the Wargrave church and schools will be held in the Town Ilall, Earlestown, on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday next. An interesting feature about the bazaar is that the hall will be lighted by electricity on the evening of each of the days named. There will be a large quanlity of goods for sale, and as the sub- ject is a worthy one, it is hoped the patronage will be numerous. ST. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL. The teachers connected with the above school had their annual picnic on Saturday. Leaving Earlestown at 8.45, the party numbering about 30, reached Blackpool about 1i o'clock, dinner being soon afterwards served at Broughton's Restaurant The various places of interest in the town were visited, including the Eiffel tower, Winter Gardens, &c., and after a most enjoyable day the party re- turned home, leaving Blackpool at 7 and reaching Earlestown about 9.30. Toe arrangements were efficiently carried out by the Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, Messrs. Latimer and Martindale. A CHURCH DIFFICULTY AT HAYDOCIC. A difference, which at present is in eratro, has broken out in Church matters at Haydock, the note of discord being in reference to the ritual observed at St. James's Church. It may here be stated that for many years past the form ot service at the church has been in the " High" direction, and up to within the past week,has apparently given satis- faction to the parishioners. Suddenly, however, it has been discovered that the ritual is not exactly as it should be, and consequently opposing parties have taken the field, one being in layout of the existing form of service, and the other Contending for a much lower observance. One or two meet- ings have been held. and it will be interesting to watch the development of the agitation. VOLUNTEER PRIZE MEETING AT NEWTON. div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY &T EA.RLESTOWN.

The filling of the vacancy in Crowe-lane ward, caused by the death of Councillor James Smith turned out to be a bloodless victory for the .Conser- vative party. It was rumoured when the seat be- came vacant,that there would he several candidate, but the!rumour turned out to be:without foundation. To my mind these unopposed elections show apathy on the part of the ratepayers, and a wan*. of inter- est in the affairs of the townships, and I do not think that any vacancy which occurs should be al- lowed to be filled without opposition. The state of parties on the Council remains unchanged by the election of Dr. Patterson, and this,' suppo,e, is how matters will continue unless more interest is evinced in the town,t,ip's affairs

What we want here is a strong Ratepayers Association. They can run one at Newton,and Nhy a similiar organisation cannot be Rot together in Earlestown, I cannot quite make out. By means of their Association the people of Newton can pretty well have matters all their own way. For instance, it has been e.ecided to pave certain streets in the township which are not at the present time in a very cleanly condition. The orders given so far are ter four streets, and out of these, three are at New- ton, and one at Earlestown. 1 suppose this is what will 11),. called an equalisation of improvements, and whilst we are wallowing in mud this people of New- ton will be able to promenade in perfect security and cleanliness. A strong Ratepayers' Association cJuld alter tnis.

I see they arts agitating for a magistrate at Bar- tonwood. The agitation originated with the Parish Council; a prominent member, who is manager of a colliery, bringing the matter forward and suggest- ing that a petition to the Chancellor of the Duchy should be drawn up and signed. The Chairman of the council did not think 'hey had any gentlemen in the parish capable of undertaking the arduous duties,but naturally this was not the opinion of the originator of the petition, and to show that he meant busints,s he got a petition drawn up and had it circulated for signatures, but he omitted:to insert the name of the person he would recommend as magistrate. The people of Burtonwood have also drawn up a petition, and with an idea to business have inserted the name of Mr. R. Forshaw, brewer, Collins Green, and it is being numerously signed.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A CARTER AT
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A CARTER AT
WIN WICK.

An inquest was conducted by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy in the Parade R wm, Irlam-at., on Tuesday a coroner, fterno o n touching the death of Tuornag smith Wardle, a carter, residing at 58, Sriarpe-st., Warrington, who was killed at Winwick on Monday,—George Wardle, son ' of the deceased stated that his father was a carter in the employ of Mr. Cross, builder, Warrington. He Raw the deceased at ten minutes to five in his room on Mon- day morning. The deceased was in good health at the time. He was a steady, sober man.—Alfred France, 21, Oliver-st., a lah-urer, stated that he was at Winwick on Monday morning at 11 20. He saw two carts in Water-lane. When the first cart had passed witness, he saw a man under the wheels of the second ca t. Witness went to him. He had a spot of blood 'on his left eye and was lace downward 3. He was then dead. The wheel of the cart -vas wedged in his elbow. With assistance he removed the deceased to the edge of th 3 road. The reins wera fastened round his neck and wrist. He did not see how the deceased got under the cart wheel.—By inspector Spinks :: The Brewery cart which was in front of deceased's cart had not passed by it.—P.C. Groarke stationed at Winwick stated that he was sent for at his station shortly before twelve o'clock. He went to the scene of the accident and found the de- ceased lying there. He was then dead. Witness had the body removed to the deceased's home.—BY the Coroner : This occurred in Winwick : how is it that you brought the bode to Warrington ?—Wit - toss : I tried to get it taken in at the Swan me, Winwick, but the landlord would not hav it.—A jury- man aaked whether a publican was not obliged to find accommodation for the body.—The Coroner said the landlord was not compelled to take a dead body in, any more than anyone else. If the man bad been alive, the case would have been different—Tim Coroner remarked that the reference was that the deceased was riding on the cart and fell off The question was whether it was accidental. A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned.

Sarah Tibbells. described as a respectable.lonking woman, was fined £2O and costs in the Liverpool Plies Court Court on Thursday for using premises in Edge-hill for betting purposes, the alternative beigg two mouths' imprisonment.

div.head: TOWN CLERKSHIP OF BRADFORD.
div.p: THE TOWN CLERKSHIP OF BRADFORD.

At a meeting on Tuesday of the special com- mittee of the Bradford Corporation which has in band the appointment of a successor to the late Mr. W. T. McGowe.n,as town clerk of the borough, the number of candidates was reduced to six. The aTIPS and qualifications of the gentlemen selected ore aq follows :—Mr. F. M. Bowey, Sunderland, age 53, solicitor for 28 years, and town clerk of Sunder- hoid for 13 years. Mr. J. H. Farmer, Bootle,age 46, fuoicitor for 15 years, and town clerk of Bootle for 13 years. Mr. George McGuire,Tork, age 34,solicitor for 12 years, town clerk of York, regiitrar and deputs-judg., of York Court of Record,and secretary to the Ouse Navigation Trustees. Mr.A. Nicholson, Oldham, age 45, solicitor for 14 years. town clerk of Oldham and clerk of the peace for 13 years. Mr. Edward R. Pickmere, M.A., Liverpool, age 41, soli- citor for 14 years,assistant town clerk for 11 Years, and .now deputy town clerk for Liverpool. Mr. T. Davies Williams, L. 14.8 ,Southport, age 34, solicitor for 10 years, town clerk of Southport. prosecuting solieitor,ancl clerk to School Attendance Committee for five years. The selected candidates will have personal interviews with the special committee on Mociday next,and a recommendation will be made by the committee to the full Council later in the afternoon of the same day.

div.head: SAD DIZATII OF AN OLD WOMAN.
div.p: SAD DIZATII OF AN OLD WOMAN.

Mr. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest in the Board Itlona at the Workhouse on Monday after- noon, touching the death of Ann Sutcliffe, 75 years of age, who died in the Workhouse Infirmary on Satuiday morning.—The first witness called was Elizabeth Ann Sutchffe who stated that the deceased was her mother-in-law, and she had lived at 31, Powys-street. Deceased had been ailing for a good many years. On Monday last week, she went on a visit to Rolleston-street, and fell down. —Mary Ann CArlisle, Rolleston-street, deposed that the deceased came to visit her at 1.30 on Monday afternoon the previous week. She was then very tired. On leaving at 7.30, she fell in the doorway and hurt her arm and shoulder. The deceased had become" dizzy."—Dr. Braide, in a letter to the Coroner, stated that the cause of death was senile decay, hastened by shock and injury to arm.—Nurse Slade stated that deceased was admitted into the Workhouse Infirmary on the 19-,h and was attended by Dr. Braide. She died at 11.20 a.m. on the 22nd inst.--The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."—Mr. Hawthorn, a juryman,sugve.sted that a rider might be added to the verdict,stating that it was one of those cases in , which there was no cause for an inquiry.—The Deputy Coroner said it was not a case in which the deceased had died from natural causes. If she had died from natural causes it was at the discretion of the Coroner whether an inquest was held or not. But in this case death was accelerated by an acci- dent, and be was bound to hold an inquest.
WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held in the office of the Clerk, tlw wsey Chambers, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. William Houghton, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present : Messrs. J. Houghton, T. Halton, and S. Sutton (clerk), William Owen (surveyor), Dr, Seph- ton (medical officer), and F. Bertoos (nuisance inspec- tor).
THE VICAR OF BURTONWOOD AND THE SEWAGE QUESTION.

The Local Government Board requested that they might be furnished with the observations of the War- rington Rural District Council upon the enclosed copy of a letter which the Board had received from the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, of St. Miehael's Vicarage, Biortonwood. The letter referred to ran as follows:—" The Sanitary Authority is shamefully neglecting its duty in this parish. The stench from the filtering beds and the brook into which they empty themselves is at times intolerable. I venture to enclose a short cutting from our "Parish Chronicle" and to beg your immediate attention to the matter."—The Chairman said he had been of the opinion that the matter was in the hands of the Burton wood Parish Council,—Mr. Owen pointed out that that was not so. The estimate of Messrs. Beck tt and Company for carrying out the work in connection with the scheme had been accepted by the Rural CoLneil and the work was being proceeded with. As soon as it was completed the Parish Council would take it over.—The Chairman thought that would be a sufficient reply to the Local Government Board.—Mr. Owen said tne Parish Council had hesitated at taking the sewage arrangements over, but he had a letter from the Council stating that they were prepared to take over the sewage works when the alterations had been completed.—Mr. Halton suggested that the Clerk migl.t intorm the Local Government Board that Mr. Mitchell was responsible for what appeared in the Burtonwood magazine.—The Clerk said he would like to ask the Nuisance Inspector whether there was any ground tor the c. mplaint.—Mr. Kerfoot said there was just cause for complaint.—The Clerk said he would be glad to know from the surveyor whether it was likely when the improvements were carried out that the nuisance would tie abated.—After a little further discussion it was decided to inform the Local Government Board what stspa were being taken in the matter.

div.head: 'MB HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: 'MB HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Dr. Sephton reported that during the past month the births were 32 and deaths 19. The death rate from all causes was equal to 18 6 per 1,000 agaior, 14•1 average of the last three inoinths and 1213 the corresponding month of last year. The death rate tram zymotic dis- eases was equal to 2.8 per 1.000 against nil the average rate of the last three months and against 14 the corres- ponding month of last year. Two infectious cases of scarlet fever were reported.—The report was adopted.

div.head: SANK BROOK AGAIN.
div.p: SANK BROOK AGAIN.

Mr. Halton wished to know whether anything could be done to abate the nuisance caused by Sankey Brook. It was growing worse daily,and he tnought it was time something was done in the matter.—The Chairman : You may call it S. Helens brook.—Mr. Halton said it made him ill when travelling over it the other day. It was in a filthy dirty condition, and he did not know how people lived near to it at Sankey Bridges.—The Chairman remarked that the question had been before the Council and the previous authority and they had always felt practically powerless with regard to it, from the fact that the pollutiun was caused at Sc. Helens.—Mr. Halton asked whether the Council could not compel the offenders to abate the nuisance.—The Clerk said that course could be taken.— Dr. Sephton said the rain waslicd the chemical refuse and other effensive matter on the banks into the brook. —Mr. Halton said it must surely cause fevers.—Dr. Sephtou said he did not think so because they found that the fevers in the district were mostly scarlet fevers and these could not be directly attributable to the brook. —Mr. Halton said they had bad typhoid fever its the dis- trict.—Dr. Sephton said that was some years ago, and he thought the district compared favourably with the others in that respect. There was one thing which might be done, and that was covering the brook over and thus preventing the smell from entering the houses on the banks. It could easily be ma e into a covered sewer. —The Clerk said he know the brook had been inspected by medical gentlemen from the Local Government Board and he had some recollection that a favourable report was made on the healthy condition oh the inhabitants on the banks. Nothing could be traced directly to the brook as tending to increase the zymotic diseases.—Dr. Sepliton said he made a report to that authority fifteen years ago as to the health of the people on the banks. He found that there was aot a greater amount of moi- tality in that district from zymotic diseases than in places further away from the brook. Although the people looked sallow and poorly there was no more sick- ness amongst the people living on the banks. —Mr. Halton said during the last 15 years th 2 population had grown considerably. He thought the condition of the brook was worse now than ever it had been.—The sub- ject then dropp, d. THE SURVEYOR'S REPORT.

The SURVEYOR in his monthly report said the follow- ing plans were in accordance with the byelaws, and might be approved : Mr. H. Ezard, two blocks c-f semi- detached houses in Cinnamon-lane.Padgate ; Mr. William Byron. erection in Heath-lane, Penketh ; Mr. James Higham, new house. Sandy-lane. Ortord. With regard to the Buttonwood drainage, the estimate of Messrs. Beckett and Co. of £ll9 7s. had been accepted in accord- ance with instructions received, and the contractor was now at work —Mr. J. N. Muspratt,clerk to the Asylum's Boatd,wrote statimg that the Board could not see its way to defray any portion of the cost of putting it the new drain.—The ',Tort was adopted on the motion of Mr. John Houghton, seconded by Mr. Halton, SANKEY DRAINS. --

Two tenders were fJpened by the Chairman for the work of laying drains near the Sloop Inn, Sankey Bridges, and at Penketr -lane end. The estimate of Mr. F. T. Bennie, of Liverpool-road, was £44 2g., and that of Mr. William Heaton £45 9. 61.—The tender of Mr. Bennie was accepted. This concluded the business.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY
div.p: GREAT SANKEY

SCHOOL BOARD MEETING.—The monthly meeting of the members of the Great Sankey School Board was held on Tuesday evening in the Board-room of the Board Schools. Mr. W. P. Skelton presided, and there were nresent—the Rev. E. S. Jackson, Messrs. Wright and Fairclougls, the Clerk (Mr. W. D. Jeans, jun.). and Mr. 0. Clarke (headmaster). The Clerk reported that he had received forms from the Local Government Board relating to the Agricultora.l Ratine act, and was requested by the Board to fill up the schedules and forward to the proper authorities. The Clerk mentioned that the term of office of the old 11,ard would shortly expire, and the following new members had been elec, ed to the Board :—Mr. T. Halton Vine Cottage, Great Sankey ; the Lt,.y. E. S. Jackson, and Mr. J• Kilshaw, Cow-lane, Great Sant:ey.— me Rev. E. S. Jackson moved that a vote of thanks be accorded to the Chairman for his services during the past three years. He remarked that the business had always been conducted amicably,expeditiously, and suc- cessfully, both to the benefit of the school and the rate- payers generally.-- Mr. Wright seconded the resolution. and said he fully endorsed every remark that had been made by the rev. eectlemac.—The Schoolmaster (141r.Ci. Clarke) said he had always met with consideration at the hands of the retiring members and Chairman. Dor- log the time Mr. Skelton had been on the Board, the school had almost treble') itself in numbers.—The Clerk also thanked the Chairman for his courtesy and general kindness in all matters with which he had had to deal, or which he had to bring before the Chairman —The re- solution was unanimously carried.—The Chairman, iu responding, said in each position that he hed held on the Board,as member,vice-chairman and lastly as chairman, he had endeavoured to work for the benefit ot the school and to keep down the rates, and at the same time to keep the sehool in its highest efficiency. fle certainly bad been ably seconded by a willing Board and a willine staff. He hoped that the forthcoming Board would suc- cessfully carry on the work of the school during their term of office.and be as successfui as the previous Board had been. (Hear, hear.)—The meeting then concluded.

wycLIFFE P S. k —QUARTERLY MEETING

The quarterly opening meeting of the abovo society was held in Wycliffe Church on SandaV. There was an excellent attendance, many memhers of the "weaker sex "accompanying their male relatives. The fey. John Yonge made his first appearance at the most:lllgs iiic his illness, aril occupied the chair. Devotional exerci3es were conducted by Mr. Thomas Wallington and Mr. Healy tit. which Mr. Piernoint, of Runcorn, eave a fine rendition on the cornet of " rnou art Passing Hence."

The Chairman said h, need hardly say how glad he was to be in the church that afternoon. He could assure them that in the lon,c,r number of weeks—four months of them—he had been away from his work he had missed nothing more than he had missed the P.S.A. meetings. (Applause.) He had lo,ked forward to his return to the P.S.A. brotherhood. They had had a hot summer and many tne!ti eg moments and if one or two things he heard were true there had been a melting influenae on the attendance of the brethren for the last couple of months. It was not a very bracing day that day but he was glad that so many were there and he trusted that as anPunin came on,the attendances would not only come haek but exceed those of the past. He would not be doing them justice if he did not say how very much he thanked them for the expreseiens of sympathy they had been good ennuch to send him during his absence. He felt that Vic prayers of the brotherhood and of his own people at the church had had a deal to do with his 'being brought back to them in possession of health and strength. He was o:d-fashioned enough to believe in prayer and that God heard it and answered it. (Applause.) Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. R. H. Pearson then gave a cornet and violin duet "For all Eternity," which was well received, and with a closing hymn the Meeting ter- minated.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COUNTY FOOTBALL UNION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COUNTY FOOTBALL UNION.

A eeneral meeting of the Union took place on Tuesiay night at the Spread Eagle Hotel,in Manchester, Mr. J. E. Warren,of Warrington, in the chair. Twelve candidates were nominated for the seven vacant seats on the com- mittee. Messrs. R. Walmsley (Salford), T. Baxter (Morecambe), J. Mills (Swinton), W. Ellison (St. Helens), H. Rig e (Rochdale St. Clements), B. Ashton ( Werneth), and L. Rhodes (Crompton) were elected. Mr. J. Gaskell (Walkdon) and Mr. J. C. Buckley (Old- ham) were elected auditors.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.

_ The annual meeting of the Northern Rugby Union was held at Elti'cldersfield on Thursday night, under the presi- deney of Mr. Waller, of Brighouse. The report expressed pride at the result of the first year's working. The Union commenced with twenty-two clubs. This num- ber had been increased to fifty nine. The maj irity of the clubs had benefited financially from the formation of the Union, but owing to various causes there was a de- ficit of nearly £lOO on the funds of the Union. This need not discourage them, for future'semi-final and final ties would place them in a sound financial position. One of the reasons for the formation of the Union was that the rules framed by the Rugby Union for ideal amateur- ism were totally unworkable in this part of the country, where they had to rely on working-class players, and the ne w union was formed with the special view to riveting the requirements of thm working men players. The Chairman remarked that those who previously governeJ Rugby tootba:l believed in retrogression, and the Northern Union believed in pro- gression. The greatest unanimity had at all time pro• vailed in the'management of the uaion;and he predicted a successful future.—An important amendment to the rules of the game, proposed by the chairman, in effect was to substitute for the present method of throwing the ball out of touch a rule providing that the throwr shall rave both feet on the touch line and both hands on the ball, and throw the ball in any direction except for- ward, bat no goal could be scored from the throw out unless the ball bad passed through more than one player's hands. The opposite side might charge from anywhere on or behind t4.la line parallel with the goal line, but if any player cr!es before the ball has left the thrower's hands the referee shall allow a tree kick five yards from the touch line.—The proposal was re- jected, after discussion, the general feeling being that it was inadvisable to spring such a radical change suddenly on clubs, and that it would be better to dcfer the matter for future consideration.

div.head: LANCASTER ASYLUMS BOARD.
div.p: LANCASTER ASYLUMS BOARD.
THE WINvVICK ASYLUM.

The quarterly meeting of the Lancaster Asylums Board was held at the Co .nty Hall. Preston, Alderman T. Schofield, of Rochdale, presiding. It was resolved that Mr. William Roberts be appointed a representative on the county borough of Liverpool on the board, in place of Mr. Ripley resigned.—AldermAn Barrett then moved the adoption of the report of the Winwick Plans Commit- tee. He said it had been thought desirable to ascertain whether it were possible tor Winwick Hall to be used as an asylum for Piot children, so as to keep them separate from the adults in the asylum, and plans were prepared under the direction of Dr. Wieglesworth for the necessary alterations and additions. These had been submitted to the Lunacy Commissioners and were , practically proved by them. At the last meeting of the board £2,000 Was granted out of the asylums for this purpose, and the committee now recommended that a further £3OO be granted for the same purpose from the same fund.—Mr. J. FL Morgan seconded the motion. :In reyly to queries. Alderman Barrett said the hall would accommodate about 50 children, the average cost being about £4O per head. The report also recommended that a contribution of £2OO be made to the Warrington Corporation for laying la gas main to the hall, wnich it would be or cepoary to light with gas until the new ! a4ylem was completed. The Corporation had expended something like £l,OOO in laying that main, and the com- faittee cotvidered that the proposed grant was not an unreasonable one. The committee alQo re,,,mmended in the report approval of the tender 01 £1,996 194. 10,f. by Messrs. Holine and King of Liverpool. tor constructing the bridge under Water-lane and of £3,063 by Mr. J. A. 11 Ewalt, of Warrington, for a railway sidine. They 'further recommended that the oelk be instructed to apply to the Local Government Board for eonset.t te borrow £8,150 for the works at IVinwiek.—Tne report was adopted.—Mr. J. B. Morgan mentioned the fact that the city of Liverpool had made no payment on account of the precept of £10,238 is. 3,1. due on the Ist May for the first half-year.—The board then adjourned. •

THE TRANSVAAL RAIDERS: RELEASE OF MAJOR COVENTRY. Major Coventry, one of Dr. Jameson's officers, was released from Holloway Gaol at four o'cl,clx on Saturday atternoon, by order of the Home Secretary. It is under- stood that during the last few days representations cc n- veyed to the Home Office by the medical officer of the prison, respecting the health of Major Coventry, who was wounded at the battle of Krugersdorp, have been under Sir M. W. Ridley's careful consideration, and as the result of the report of the medical officer the Home Secretary decided to advise the release of the prisoner. Major Coventry left Holloway in a cab. His sentence,it will be remembered, was one of five m .nths' imprison- ment, and he has actually served twenty-five days. Dr. Jameson and his remaining comrades continue in good health, and are said to be in excellent spirits.
